is-private-health-insurance-worth-it.text: Pick your state, your household and the age of the oldest person covered: the calculator finds the income from which hospital cover costs less than the surcharge. On the tax side alone, private hospital cover is worth it once the Medicare levy surcharge you would pay without it is larger than what the policy costs after the rebate. Below the 2026-27 threshold of $105,000 for a single person or $210,000 for a family there is no surcharge, so cover never pays for itself through tax. Above it, the answer turns on the policy you buy. With the cheapest exempt single policy in New South Wales, $102.60 a month before the rebate in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, cover is cheaper from $105,100. With a policy at the median price, $186.10 a month, the line moves to $164,500. A Lifetime Health Cover loading pushes it further out, since the rebate is never paid on the loading. Whether the cover is worth it for your health is a separate question that this page does not try to answer. Two questions hidden in one People who type "is private health insurance worth it" usually mean two things at once. The first is a money question: will a hospital policy cost me more than the tax I pay without one? The second is a health question: will the policy pay out when I need it, for the treatment I care about? Only the first has an answer that holds for everybody with the same income, state and family, because it rests on published rules and published prices. This page answers that one, and it answers it in dollars. The money question has three moving parts. The Medicare levy surcharge you pay without cover rises with your income, from 1 % to 1.5 %. The rebate lowers the premium but falls as your income rises, and disappears at tier 3. The Lifetime Health Cover loading raises the premium if you join after your base day. All three are set from the same income tiers, so they have to be computed together, not one after the other. The break-even income for a single person in NSW Read the table from the top. Under $105,000 there is nothing to compare: no surcharge, and the policy is a pure cost on the tax side. Just above the threshold, the surcharge is 1 % of your income and the cheapest policy, after the tier 1 rebate of 16.079 %, is already a little cheaper. The median policy only wins at incomes where the surcharge has grown to 1.5 %, and a Silver policy at the median Silver price wins from $164,500. Why the rebate works against you as income rises The rebate is not a fixed discount. For a person under 65 it is 24.118 % at the base tier, 16.079 % at tier 1, 8.038 % at tier 2 and nothing at tier 3. So the net price of the same policy goes up exactly when the surcharge goes up. That is why the gap between the two does not simply widen with income: at the step into tier 3 the surcharge rate rises to 1.5 % and the rebate falls to zero at the same moment. The thresholds page shows the exact boundaries. Older households get more rebate. When the oldest person on the policy is 70 or over, the base tier rebate is 32.158 %, which lowers the break-even income. A bill before Parliament would bring the over 65 rates down to the under 65 ones from 1 April 2027; it is not law, and the over 65 page prices the change. The loading changes the sum for late joiners A person who first takes out hospital cover at 50 pays 40 % more on the hospital premium for ten years, and the rebate does not reduce that extra. On $140,000 in NSW the cheapest policy then costs $1,625 a year against a surcharge of $1,750. Cover still wins, but by less. The loading ends after ten continuous years, while the surcharge is due every year you stay uncovered above the threshold, so a single year's comparison understates the case for joining. The base day page shows what each year of delay adds. Couples and families For a couple the tier comes from combined income, tested against $210,000, and both partners and every dependant must be covered to avoid the surcharge: PrivateHealth.gov.au says plainly that if your partner or one of your dependants is not covered, you will pay it. A couple policy costs about twice a single one, and the surcharge is charged on both incomes, so the break-even depends on how the income is split. Set the household in the calculator and enter your partner's income; the result is your own income from which the cheapest family policy costs less. The couples page and the families page go through the cases. What the numbers cannot tell you A cheap Basic policy that removes the surcharge can leave you without cover for treatments you might want as a private patient. Every policy has a Private Health Information Statement that lists what it covers and excludes, and PrivateHealth.gov.au publishes the statement of every policy on sale. Our comparison stops at the tax line on purpose. If the cheapest exempt policy is all you want, the sum above is the whole story; if you want cover you would actually use, put its premium in the calculator and see what it really costs you after the surcharge it saves. At what income does private hospital cover pay for itself? Only above the surcharge threshold, $105,000 for a single in 2026-27. In NSW the cheapest exempt single policy beats the surcharge from $105,100; a median-priced policy only from $164,500. The tool above gives the line for your state, household, age band and loading, holding a partner's income fixed. Why does the answer change so much with the policy chosen? Because the surcharge is fixed by your income while the premium is set by the policy. A single on $140,000 pays $1,750 of surcharge in 2026-27. The cheapest exempt NSW policy costs $1,132 after the rebate, a median one $2,054. Same income, same tax, two opposite answers. Does a Lifetime Health Cover loading make cover a bad deal? It makes it dearer, not necessarily a bad deal. Someone joining at 50 carries a 40 % loading, so the cheapest NSW policy costs $1,625 a year at $140,000 instead of $1,132. The loading goes after 10 continuous years, while the surcharge comes back every year you stay uncovered above the threshold. Is waiting a few years before buying cover a saving? Rarely, once you are past your base day and above the threshold. The waiting calculator puts three years of waiting from age 31 on $115,000 at $4,189 in NSW: more loading for ten years plus the surcharge in the meantime, after the premium you would not have paid. Under the threshold, waiting costs only the growing loading. What does this page leave out of the worth it question? Everything that is not tax: the treatments a policy covers, waiting periods, gap payments, choice of doctor and hospital, and how you weigh public hospital waiting times. Those depend on the policy and on your health. Our figures answer one narrow question, whether the policy costs more or less than the surcharge, so you can then judge the rest on its own merits.

lifetime-health-cover-loading.text: Enter your age on the 1 July before you take out hospital cover: the loading, and its price on the cheapest policy of your state, appear at once. The Lifetime Health Cover loading is an extra 2 % on the hospital part of your premium for every year you were over 30 on the 1 July before you first took out hospital cover. Someone who joins at 40 pays 20 % more than a person who joined by the deadline, someone who joins at 45 pays 30 %, and the figure stops at 70 % however late you start. Your deadline is your LHC base day, the 1 July after your 31st birthday. The loading is not permanent: it is removed once you have held hospital cover for 10 continuous years, and you may spend up to 1,094 days without cover over your life without it growing. It applies to hospital cover only, never to extras, and the government rebate is not paid on it. On the cheapest single policy in New South Wales, $1,231 a year before the rebate, a 20 % loading adds $246 a year, about $2,462 over the ten loaded years at today's premium. The rule in four lines PrivateHealth.gov.au, the Ombudsman's consumer site, sets out the rule in a few sentences, and the ATO repeats it on its page about the loading. Read together, they come to this: The base day is the 1 July after your 31st birthday. Take out hospital cover before it and you never pay a loading. Every year you were over 30 on the 1 July before joining adds 2 % . The loading cannot exceed 70 % . It is removed after 10 years of continuous hospital cover, and you can be without cover for 1,094 days in your life without penalty. The point that catches people is the date that counts. It is not your age on the day you sign, but your age on the 1 July before it. A person who turns 41 in August and joins in September is loaded on age 40, so 20 %, not 22 %. Joining before your next 1 July therefore stops the meter for a full year. What the percentage costs in dollars A percentage tells you little until you put a premium under it. The cheapest hospital policy that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge for a single person in New South Wales costs $1,231 a year before the rebate in the October 2026 data. On that premium a 30 % loading, the figure for someone joining at 45, adds $369 a year. Over the ten loaded years it comes to about $3,694 at today's price, and more in practice, since premiums rose 4.41 % on average on 1 April 2026. The loading follows the policy you choose. On a Gold hospital policy at three or four times the price of a Basic one, the same percentage costs three or four times as much. That is one reason late joiners often start with a cheap policy that is enough to avoid the surcharge, then move up once the ten years have passed. Moving up does not restart the count. Couples and families: the loading is averaged On a policy that covers two adults, the insurer averages the two loadings. PrivateHealth.gov.au gives the case of Lukas, who joins at 41 with a loading of 22 %, and his partner Noor, who has held cover since her twenties and has none. Their couple policy carries 11 %.lhc(41), 0)}. The same averaging covers every adult on the policy. PrivateHealth.gov.au gives the case of Lucy, a dependant with a disability who joins her parents' family cover at 33 with her own 6 %: spread across three adults, the family policy carries 2 %. Gaps: the 1,094 days Once you hold hospital cover after your base day, you can drop it for up to 1,094 days in total across your life, roughly three years, without any change. If you cancel to live overseas for at least a year, the days abroad do not count towards them, and neither do days on a suspension your insurer approves. Past the allowance, the loading resumes: 2 % on top of what you had, plus 2 % for every further year without cover. The details are on the days of absence page . What the loading is not It is not a tax and not the Medicare levy surcharge. The surcharge is charged by the ATO on your tax return each year you earn over the threshold without hospital cover. The loading is charged by your insurer inside your premium, once you do take cover. They pull in the same direction: one is a reason to join, the other a reason to join early. The page is private health insurance worth it weighs them together. Exceptions that change your base day New arrivals in Australia are given time. If you were not eligible for full Medicare cover on your base day, you have until the later of that day and the first anniversary of your full Medicare registration to take out hospital cover without a loading; the new migrants page has the dates. Australian citizens and permanent residents who were overseas on their base day have until the first anniversary of their return, and short trips home of up to 90 days do not end their time abroad (see returning from overseas ). People born on or before 1 July 1934 are exempt altogether. Your insurer is the one that applies the loading, from the information you give and from a transfer certificate when you switch funds. When you switch, your former insurer must give you a clearance certificate within 14 days, and that document carries your loading and your dates. If you think your percentage is wrong, ask the insurer which dates it used and compare them with the Ombudsman rules . How the figures on this page are built The rule comes from PrivateHealth.gov.au (Ombudsman), Lifetime Health Cover and ATO, Lifetime health cover loading , both read on 19 October 2026. The premiums come from the PrivateHealth.gov.au product file of 1 October 2026, published on data.gov.au under a Creative Commons licence: we keep the open hospital policies whose excess stays within the surcharge limits and take the cheapest one per state and cover type. The method page lists every filter. How is the Lifetime Health Cover loading worked out? Take your age on the 1 July before the day you first buy hospital cover, subtract 30, and multiply by 2 %. A person aged 39 on that 1 July has a loading of 18 %, which is the example PrivateHealth.gov.au gives. The result is capped at 70 %, reached at age 65. Your insurer applies it to the hospital part of every premium. Is the LHC loading charged on extras cover? No. The loading falls only on hospital cover, the part of a policy that pays for treatment as a private patient in hospital. Extras such as dental, optical or physiotherapy are not loaded, and holding extras alone does not stop a loading from building up. On a combined policy, the insurer splits the premium and loads only the hospital share. Does the private health insurance rebate apply to the loading? No. The rebate is a percentage of the base premium only. If your hospital premium is $2,000 and your loading is 10 %, you pay $200 of loading in full and the rebate is worked out on the $2,000 alone. The ATO gives the same example with a $200 loading on which no rebate is paid. How do I get rid of a Lifetime Health Cover loading? Keep hospital cover for 10 continuous years after the loading starts. Switching insurer or product keeps the count running when the cover is continuous; permitted gaps do not break it but do not count towards it. After those ten years the loading drops to zero. If you later cancel and stay uncovered beyond your 1,094 permitted days, a new loading can apply when you come back. Who never pays a Lifetime Health Cover loading? Anyone who takes out hospital cover by their LHC base day and keeps it, people born on or before 1 July 1934, and anyone treated as holding hospital cover, such as a veteran listed on a DVA Gold Card or an ADF member on continuous full-time service. New migrants have until the later of their base day and the first anniversary of full Medicare registration.

mls-110000.text: A single income of $110,000 sits just above the 2026-27 threshold. The calculator compares the 1 % surcharge with the cheapest policy for your state, age and loading. A single person whose income for MLS purposes is $110,000 in 2026-27 is $5,000 over the threshold of $105,000, which puts them in tier 1. Without an appropriate level of hospital cover for the whole year, the surcharge is 1 % of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits: $1,100 if all $110,000 is of that kind. Crossing the threshold also cuts the rebate on any policy you hold, from 24.118 % to 16.079 % for people under 65. Even so, the cheapest exempt single policy costs less than the surcharge in every state in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, though only just in some: in New South Wales $1,033 a year after the rebate, $67 under the surcharge; in the Northern Territory $396. A loading from a late start can tip the balance the other way at this income. State by state at $110,000 The surcharge is the same everywhere, $1,100, because it is a federal tax. Premiums are not. In the east the margin is thin: in Queensland the cheapest exempt policy saves $63 a year, which a modest premium rise on 1 April could erase. In Western Australia and the Northern Territory the gap is wide. Five thousand dollars over the line At this income the question people ask is whether they can get back under $105,000. Income for MLS purposes is taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits, reportable super contributions and net investment losses. Salary sacrificing into super does not help, since the sacrificed amount comes back in as a reportable super contribution. Deductions you are entitled to do lower taxable income, and so the income tested. The income for MLS purposes page lists every item, and the salary packaging page covers the fringe benefits case. If you already hold cover: the rebate step For someone who already has hospital cover, crossing $105,000 costs nothing in surcharge but something in rebate. On the cheapest NSW single policy, $1,231 a year before the rebate, the fall from 24.118 % to 16.079 % means about $99 more to pay. On a policy three times dearer, three times as much. The rebate entitlement is settled on your tax return from your actual income for the year, so a pay rise in March can still move you into tier 1 for the whole period from 1 July. Update your income tier with your insurer when you expect to cross the line: it avoids a bill when you lodge. Age changes the rebate, not the surcharge The surcharge at $110,000 is the same at 30 or at 70. The rebate is not: at tier 1 it is 16.079 % under 65, 20.098 % from 65 to 69 and 24.118 % from 70, based on the oldest person on the policy. A single person aged 68 in NSW would pay $984 for the cheapest policy after the rebate, against the same $1,100 of surcharge. For a couple, an income of $110,000 on its own is far below the family threshold of $210,000: the surcharge only applies if the combined income is over that line, which is the subject of the couples page . Joining part way through the year The surcharge is charged by the day. Someone at $110,000 who takes out hospital cover on 1 January pays about $552 for the six months without it, not $1,100. What has already passed cannot be undone, but every month of cover from now on replaces a month of surcharge. The part-year page compares joining now with staying uncovered to 30 June. What changes next year Thresholds are indexed each 1 July. The 2026-27 line of $105,000 was $101,000 in 2025-26, so an income that does not rise can fall back under the threshold in a later year. Premiums and rebate rates change on 1 April. A comparison made at $110,000 today is worth redoing each year, especially here, where the gap between the two options is a few dollars a week. How much Medicare levy surcharge is due on $110,000? $1,100 for a full year without hospital cover in 2026-27, if the whole $110,000 is taxable income and reportable fringe benefits. The tier 1 rate is 1 %. If part of your income for MLS purposes is super contributions or investment losses, those count for the tier but the rate is charged only on the rest. Why does my rebate fall when I earn $110,000? Because the rebate uses the same income tiers as the surcharge. At $110,000 you are in tier 1, where a person under 65 receives 16.079 % instead of 24.118 %. Tell your insurer: the ATO warns that claiming too much rebate as a premium reduction can leave you with a tax liability. Is the surcharge ever cheaper than cover on $110,000? Yes, when the policy is dearer than the cheapest one or carries a loading. Someone who joins at 40 has a 20 % loading; the cheapest NSW policy then costs $1,279 a year against a surcharge of $1,100. The loading ends after ten years; the surcharge recurs every year you stay above the threshold uncovered.

mls-thresholds.text: Type your income for MLS purposes and your situation: the tier, the surcharge rate and the rebate that go with it appear at once. For the 2026-27 income year, which runs from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, the Medicare levy surcharge starts above $105,000 of income for MLS purposes for a single person and above $210,000 for a couple, a family or a single parent, the family figure rising by $1,500 for each dependent child after the first. Above the base tier come three bands: tier 1 to $123,000 single or $246,000 family at 1 %, tier 2 to $164,000 or $328,000 at 1.25 %, and tier 3 beyond at 1.5 %. Each boundary is inclusive: $105,000 exactly is still the base tier. The thresholds rose by $4,000 for singles and $8,000 for families compared with 2025-26, while the rates did not move. The same tiers also set your private health insurance rebate, so one number on your tax return decides both. The rates apply only if you, your spouse or a dependant spent days without an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. The 2026-27 table The ATO publishes the thresholds as a single table with two rows, one for singles and one for families, and four columns. We reproduce it with the rebate percentage for people under 65 next to it, since the tiers are shared. A couple without children uses the family row, exactly like a couple with one child. The column is the same; only the increment for a second, third or later child changes it. What changed from 2025-26 Every boundary moved up for 2026-27. For a single person the base threshold went from $101,000 to $105,000, the top of tier 1 from $118,000 to $123,000 and the top of tier 2 from $158,000 to $164,000. The family boundaries moved from $202,000, $236,000 and $316,000 to $210,000, $246,000 and $328,000. Someone whose income stays flat can therefore drop a tier this year without doing anything: a single person on $120,000 was in tier 2 under the 2025-26 table and is in tier 1 under the new one. Which table applies is set by the income year, not by the date you lodge. A return lodged in October 2026 is for 2025-26 and uses the old figures; the new thresholds show up on the return you lodge after 30 June 2027. Several insurer and comparison pages still printed the 2025-26 figures well into the new year, which is why it pays to check the year in the heading of any table you read. Each tier is a step, not a slope The surcharge is not charged on the slice of income above a threshold, as income tax is. Once you are in a tier, its rate falls on your whole taxable income and reportable fringe benefits. Crossing a boundary therefore makes the bill jump. At $123,000 a single person without cover pays $1,230; one dollar more and the figure is $1,538, a jump of $308. At the top of tier 2 the jump to tier 3 is $410. The first step, from nothing to tier 1, is the largest of all: $1,050 appears the moment income passes $105,000. That step shape matters for anyone near a boundary. A salary sacrifice into super does not help, since reportable super contributions are added back into income for MLS purposes. A deduction that lowers taxable income does lower it. Income for MLS purposes lists what is added back and what is not. More children, higher family threshold The family row rises by $1,500 for each MLS dependent child after the first. A child counts while under 21, or from 21 to 24 while studying full time; a foster child does not count. The increase applies to all three boundaries at once. The families page shows who counts as a dependent child and what happens in the year a child turns 21 or leaves full-time study. Thresholds decide the rate, cover decides whether you pay Being above a threshold does not by itself mean you owe anything. The surcharge applies only for days on which you, your spouse or one of your dependants lacked an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. Hospital cover from a registered insurer with an excess of $750 or less for one person, or $1,500 or less on any other policy, removes it at any income. The excess page covers the details. How the ATO applies the table You do not pick a tier on your return. You report your income test items and, at question M2, the number of days for which you do not have to pay the surcharge; your insurer's private health insurance statement gives the days of cover. The ATO then works out the tier, adds any surcharge to the Medicare levy and shows both as one line, Medicare levy and surcharge, on your notice of assessment. Nothing is withheld from your pay for it during the year. Where these figures come from Every number on this page is read from ATO, Medicare levy surcharge income, thresholds and rates (updated 22 June 2026) , which carries the 2026-27 and 2025-26 tables, and is cross-checked against the PrivateHealth.gov.au surcharge page , which prints the same figures for both years. The rebate column comes from ATO, Income thresholds and rates for the private health insurance rebate (updated 22 June 2026) . Our method page explains how the calculators apply them. Are the MLS thresholds the same as the rebate income tiers? Yes. The ATO uses one set of income tiers for both. The base tier, tier 1, tier 2 and tier 3 that set your surcharge rate also set the percentage of your private health insurance rebate. At tier 3, above $164,000 single or $328,000 family, the surcharge is at its highest and the rebate falls to zero at every age. Did the MLS thresholds go up for 2026-27? Yes. The single base threshold moved from $101,000 in 2025-26 to $105,000, and the family one from $202,000 to $210,000. Every tier boundary rose by a similar step. The rates of 1 %, 1.25 % and 1.5 % stayed exactly as they were, and so did the $1,500 added for each child after the first. Which threshold applies to a single parent? The family one. PrivateHealth.gov.au states that single parents and couples, de facto couples included, are subject to the family tiers. A single parent with one dependent child is therefore tested against $210,000 for 2026-27, and the line moves up by $1,500 for each further child. The test uses the parent's own income, as there is no spouse to add. What happens if my income is exactly on a threshold? You stay in the lower tier. The ATO prints the boundaries as "or less" for the base tier and as ranges starting one dollar higher for the next tier. A single person on exactly $105,000 pays no surcharge, while one dollar more moves the whole base into tier 1 at 1 %, because the rate falls on the full income, not on the excess. When will the 2027-28 thresholds be published? They are upcoming. On 19 October 2026 the ATO page shows thresholds for 2026-27 and earlier years only. The current table was put online on 22 June 2026, a few days before its income year began on 1 July. This page will take the 2027-28 figures on the day the ATO publishes them; until then, any figure quoted elsewhere is an estimate.

private-health-insurance-rebate.text: Give your income for surcharge purposes, your premium and the age of the oldest person on the policy: the rebate comes out in dollars a year and a month. The private health insurance rebate is the government's share of your premium. From 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 it is 24.118 % of the premium at the base tier when everyone on the policy is under 65, 16.079 % at tier 1, 8.038 % at tier 2 and nothing at tier 3. The rate rises with the age of the oldest person covered: 28.139 % at the base tier between 65 and 69, 32.158 % from 70. The tier is set by your income for surcharge purposes, the same test and the same thresholds as the Medicare levy surcharge: for 2026-27, the base tier stops at $105,000 for a single person and $210,000 for a couple or a family. On the cheapest couple policy that avoids the surcharge in New South Wales, $2,462 a year before the rebate, a couple under 65 at the base tier gets $594 back. The rebate is never paid on a Lifetime Health Cover loading, and the percentages change each 1 April. Twelve percentages, one table The whole rebate fits in a grid of three age bands by four income tiers. The rows below are those of the ATO and of the Department of Health circular that set them, PHI 12/26 . The tiers are not specific to the rebate. They are the Medicare levy surcharge tiers, tested on the same income for surcharge purposes: taxable income, reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses and reportable super contributions, added for you and your spouse. For 2026-27 a single person is at the base tier up to $105,000, at tier 1 up to $123,000, at tier 2 up to $164,000, and at tier 3 beyond. For a couple, a single parent or a family the limits are $210,000, $246,000 and $328,000. Income for MLS purposes explains each item of the total. What the percentage is worth on real premiums A rate means little until it is applied to a price. Two couple policies from the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 show the range: the cheapest hospital policy for a couple in NSW that avoids the surcharge ($2,462 a year before the rebate), and the median policy of the same kind ($4,434). The gap between the top and the bottom of that table is large. A retired couple over 70 on a modest income gets $1,426 a year towards a median policy; a couple under 65 at tier 2 gets $356 on the same premium. Tier 3 households pay the full price. Your status on 30 June decides the threshold The ATO tests the rebate on your family status on the last day of the income year. If you had a spouse on 30 June, the family thresholds apply to your combined income for the whole year, even if you met in March. If you separated during the year and had no dependent child on 30 June, the single thresholds apply to your own income alone. A single parent is always tested on the family thresholds, with only their own income counted. When a spouse dies during the year and the survivor has no dependant on 30 June, the family thresholds still apply, to the incomes of both. That date rule produces surprises in both directions. A person on $110,000 who moves in with a partner on $40,000 before 30 June goes from tier 1 as a single (16.079 %) to the base tier as a couple (24.118 %), because $150,000 is under the family threshold. The reverse happens to a couple on a high joint income who separate in May. Three periods in the same calendar year Rates move on 1 April and thresholds on 1 July, so 2026 had three combinations. From 1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026, the 2025-26 thresholds (base tier up to $101,000 single) went with the old rates, 24.288 % at the base tier under 65. From 1 April to 30 June 2026, PrivateHealth.gov.au shows the new rates applied to the same old thresholds. From 1 July 2026 to 31 March 2027, the new rates go with the new thresholds of $105,000, $123,000 and $164,000. The rates from 1 April 2027 will be published in March 2027. The rebate and the loading If your premium includes a Lifetime Health Cover loading, the rebate is worked out on the premium without it. The ATO example is Rebecca: $220 for two months of cover, of which $20 is a 10 % loading. Only $200 is eligible, and at 24.288 % she gets $49. The loading page shows what that means over ten years. Who can claim it The ATO lists four conditions: a complying policy with an Australian registered insurer, eligibility for Medicare, being a private health insurance incentive beneficiary, and an income for surcharge purposes below the tier 3 threshold. Every adult the policy covers is an incentive beneficiary. If the policy covers only a dependent child, the parents are; if they are not a couple on 30 June, the one who pays the premium is. When an employer pays the premium under a salary packaging arrangement, the rebate still depends on your income, not the employer's. How the money reaches you, as a lower premium or at tax time, is on the page premium reduction or tax offset . A change to the rates for people aged 65 and over is before Parliament: the over 65 page sets out what it would cost. For a single person, the cheapest exempt policy in NSW costs $1,231 a year, and the base tier rebate under 65 takes $297 off it. What are the private health insurance rebate rates from 1 April 2026? Under 65: 24.118 %, 16.079 % and 8.038 % for the base tier, tier 1 and tier 2. From 65 to 69: 28.139 %, 20.098 % and 12.058 %. From 70: 32.158 %, 24.118 % and 16.079 %. Tier 3 gets nothing at any age. These rates run until 31 March 2027. Which policies attract the rebate? Hospital, general treatment (extras) and ambulance policies from an Australian registered health insurer, provided the policy is a complying one. Overseas Visitors Health Cover and policies from an overseas insurer not registered in Australia attract no rebate. You must also be eligible for Medicare and have an income for surcharge purposes below the tier 3 threshold. Whose age sets the rebate on a couple policy? The age of the oldest person the policy covers. A couple aged 63 and 67 gets the 65 to 69 rate on the whole premium, 28.139 % at the base tier instead of 24.118 %. The rate changes when the oldest person reaches 65 or 70, not on 1 July or 1 April. Why did my rebate fall slightly on 1 April 2026? Because the rebate adjustment factor for 2026 was 0.993. Each 1 April the percentages are multiplied by a factor that reflects the gap between inflation and the average premium increase, which was 4.41 % in 2026. The base tier rate under 65 went from 24.288 % to 24.118 %. Do my children's incomes count towards the rebate tier? No. Family income for surcharge purposes is your income and your spouse's, nothing more. Children only raise the family threshold: $1,500 for each Medicare levy surcharge dependent child after the first, so a family with three such children reaches tier 1 only above $213,000 in 2026-27.

state-nsw.text: One price list serves Sydney and Canberra. Enter a household and see the surcharge without cover against the cheapest family policy. Residents of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory choose from the same hospital policies: the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 lists no separate ACT prices, so the NSW premiums apply to both. The cheapest open policy that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge costs $102.60 a month for one person and $205.20 for a family, before the rebate, from ahm health insurance. A family with two dependent children is tested on the combined income of both parents against $211,500 in 2026-27, the $210,000 family threshold plus $1,500 for the second child. Over that line each parent pays the surcharge on their own income. On a combined $245,000, split $150,000 and $95,000, the household pays $2,450 without cover against $2,066 for the cheapest family policy after the rebate. Four households, same state Each row is a couple with two dependent children, the older parent aged 42 and no Lifetime Health Cover loading. The surcharge is the sum of what both parents would pay without cover; the policy figures are net of the rebate. The first household is just over the line and in tier 1, where the surcharge is 1 % of each income and the rebate is still 16.079 %. Even there, the cheapest family policy costs less than the tax. A policy at the median family price is another matter: it costs more than the surcharge on every row, although the gap shrinks as the tiers rise, to $82 at the last one. At that row, in tier 3, the rebate is gone and the full family premium is paid. That gap is the real choice for a Sydney or Canberra family. The cheapest policy is the cheapest way to settle the tax question. A fuller policy is a decision about health care, and the surcharge you avoid pays for part of it: on the second row, $2,450 of the $4,349 a median policy costs. The worth it page sets out that reasoning, and the cover calculator above takes your own premium in its folded options. When one parent earns little The combined test can catch a family where one parent stays at home. If the other earns $240,000 alone, the household is in tier 1 and that parent pays $2,400 without cover. The partner with an income for MLS purposes of $28,011 or less owes nothing (the 2025-26 figure; the 2026-27 one is not published yet). Cover still has to include the whole family to stop the surcharge: a single policy for the earner leaves the household liable. The families page goes through the dependants rules. Children change the threshold, not the rate. A third child lifts the family line to $213,000, a fourth to $214,500. A child is an MLS dependant while under 21, or from 21 to 24 while studying full time, which is why families with older children should check who still counts before they read the table. The family price list in NSW The cheapest family policies cost twice the single ones, $102.60 against $205.20, and the three cheapest are within a few dollars: ahm health insurance, see-u by HBF at $206.78 and GMHBA Limited at $208.10. A single parent policy, for one adult and children, starts at $156.05. Each of these is Basic tier: it avoids the surcharge, and its Private Health Information Statement says what else it pays for. Naming the cheapest policy reports a price, it is not a recommendation. Sources: PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 on data.gov.au , ATO rules on family and dependants , thresholds and rates . How the figures are built . Do ACT residents pay the same hospital premiums as NSW? In the public product file, yes: it publishes prices by state and has no ACT list, and policies sold in the ACT appear under New South Wales. Our figures for NSW therefore stand for Canberra too. The surcharge and the rebate are federal, with the same thresholds and rates in both places. How much does the cheapest family hospital policy cost in NSW? $205.20 a month before the rebate in the file of 1 October 2026, a Basic policy from ahm health insurance with an excess of $1,500 per policy. The median family policy that avoids the surcharge costs $431.86. Families have 821 open policies to choose from in the state. Does every child on the policy raise the family threshold? Every MLS dependent child after the first adds $1,500. With one child the threshold stays at $210,000; with three it is $213,000. A child counts if under 21, or 21 to 24 and studying full time. A foster child is not an MLS dependant.

income-for-mls-purposes.text: Split your income into its parts: the tool adds back what the ATO adds back and shows which part the surcharge is charged on. Income for MLS purposes is not your taxable income. The ATO starts from taxable income, leaves out any assessable first home super saver released amount, and adds four things if they apply to you: reportable fringe benefits from your income statement, reportable super contributions (employer contributions made under salary sacrifice plus personal contributions you claimed as a deduction), your total net investment loss from shares and rental property, and any amount on which family trust distribution tax was paid. For a couple, both partners' totals are added together. That sum decides your tier against the 2026-27 thresholds of $105,000 single and $210,000 family. The rate of the tier is then charged on a narrower base: taxable income, reportable fringe benefits and family trust amounts only. Super contributions and investment losses can push you into a tier without being charged themselves. The ATO case of Josh shows it: $127,000 of income for MLS purposes, but a surcharge worked out on $110,000. The ATO worksheet, row by row The paper return instructions for question M2 include a worksheet with a column for you and one for your spouse. It is the clearest statement of what the ATO counts. We follow its rows, and mark which ones also go into the base the surcharge is charged on. Row j adds the column up. For a single person, that is the income for MLS purposes. With a spouse, the two row j figures added together give the combined income tested against the family threshold of $210,000. Exempt foreign employment income goes into row a when your taxable income is at least $1. Two ATO examples, two years Tom, 2026-27. Tom is 35, single, without cover. His taxable income is $90,000 and his reportable fringe benefits $27,000, so his income for MLS purposes is $117,000. That is tier 1, and the 1 % rate falls on the whole $117,000: $1,170. Here the two bases coincide, because Tom has nothing that counts for the tier only. Josh, 2025-26. Josh is also 35, single, without cover. His taxable income is $90,000, his reportable fringe benefits $20,000 and his net investment losses $17,000. His income for MLS purposes is $127,000, tier 2 at 1.25 %, but the rate is applied to $110,000 only: $1,375. The $17,000 of losses pushed him up a tier without being charged. Under the 2026-27 thresholds the same figures still land in tier 2 and give $1,375. Where people get caught Most surprises come from add-backs that lower taxable income in one place and reappear here. Salary sacrifice. Sacrificing pay into super reduces taxable income but reappears as a reportable employer contribution. On $100,000 of taxable income with $10,000 sacrificed, the test income is $110,000: above $105,000, a surcharge of $1,000 without cover. Personal deductible contributions. The same applies to a contribution you make yourself and claim as a deduction in your return. Negative gearing. A rental loss that brings taxable income down to $98,000 is added back: $12,000 of loss gives a test income of $110,000 and a surcharge of $980, charged on the $98,000. Salary packaging. Fringe benefits count twice over, for the tier and for the base. The salary packaging page works through common packages. What does not appear in the worksheet is not added. A first home super saver amount released to you is taken out of taxable income for this purpose. A couple adds two columns, then splits the bill The combined figure only sets the tier. Each partner is then charged on their own taxable income and fringe benefits, for their own days without cover. A partner whose own income for MLS purposes is $28,011 or less is not liable when the couple was together all year (2025-26 figure; the 2026-27 one is not yet published). The couples page has the details. The same figure sets your rebate The ATO uses the same sum, under the name income for surcharge purposes, to set your private health insurance rebate. An add-back that moves you from tier 1 to tier 2 raises the surcharge rate from 1 % to 1.25 % and cuts the rebate for people under 65 from 16.079 % to 8.038 % of the premium. If you take the rebate as a reduced premium, you tell your insurer which tier you expect to be in; claim too much and you may have a tax liability when you lodge, so the ATO asks you to tell the insurer when your income moves to another tier. The rebate page explains the reconciliation. Sources The definition is on the ATO page on income for MLS purposes, thresholds and rates , updated 22 June 2026, and in the worksheet of ATO, M2 Medicare levy surcharge 2026 (tax return instructions) . The Tom example is the ATO's 2026-27 example; Josh is the 2025-26 example of the M2 instructions. Our method shows how the calculator splits the two bases. Is salary sacrifice into super counted for the Medicare levy surcharge? Yes, for the tier. Salary sacrificed contributions are reportable employer super contributions, and the ATO adds them back to income for MLS purposes. They do not enter the base the rate is charged on. Someone on $100,000 of taxable income who sacrifices $10,000 is tested on $110,000, so is above the single threshold, and pays $1,000 without cover. Does a negative gearing loss reduce income for MLS purposes? No. A net rental property loss lowers your taxable income, but the ATO adds it back when it works out income for MLS purposes, together with any net financial investment loss. A landlord with $98,000 of taxable income after a $12,000 rental loss is tested on $110,000, above the 2026-27 single threshold of $105,000. Are reportable fringe benefits charged by the surcharge or only counted? Both. Reportable fringe benefits are the one add-back that also forms part of the base the surcharge rate falls on, together with taxable income. The ATO example of Tom, who has a taxable income and a fringe benefits amount, charges the tier 1 rate on the sum of the two. Use the grossed-up figure printed on your income statement. Does foreign income count for the surcharge? Exempt foreign employment income does. The M2 instructions say to add it to taxable income when working out income for MLS purposes, provided your taxable income is $1 or more. Foreign income that is already assessable is part of taxable income anyway. Overseas cover held with a foreign fund still does not count as private patient hospital cover. What extra amount does a spouse bring into the family total? Besides their own taxable income and add-backs, a spouse brings any share of the net income of a trust on which the trustee must pay tax and which is not already in their taxable income. The ATO worksheet keeps it in a separate row of the spouse column. Your two column totals, added together, give the combined income for MLS purposes.

lhc-base-day-turning-31.text: Enter your age on 1 July 2026 and how long you would wait: the calculator adds the loading you would carry for ten years and the surcharge paid in the meantime. Your Lifetime Health Cover base day is, for most people, the 1 July following your 31st birthday. Hold private hospital cover on that day and keep it, and you will never pay a loading. Miss it, and the first policy you buy later carries 2 % extra for every year you were over 30 on the 1 July before you joined, for ten years. If you turn 31 in March 2027, your base day is 1 July 2027; if you turned 31 in September 2026, it is also 1 July 2027. Someone born in May 1995 turned 31 in May 2026 and reached their base day on 1 July 2026: buying in August 2026 already costs 2 %. On the cheapest single policy in Victoria, $1,225 a year before the rebate, each 2 % of loading adds about $25 a year. Under 31 there is no loading at all, and some insurers give younger people an age-based discount. Finding your own date The base day depends only on your date of birth, unless one of the special cases below applies. Take the date of your 31st birthday, then go forward to the next 1 July. The examples cover the people turning 31 around now. PrivateHealth.gov.au words the rule as the later of 1 July 2000 or the 1 July following your 31st birthday. The ATO puts it from the other side: you do not pay the loading if you are under 31, or if you hold an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover before your base day ( ATO ). Only private hospital cover from an Australian registered insurer counts. Extras cover, Overseas Visitors Health Cover, Overseas Student Health Cover and foreign insurance do not. What one year of hesitation costs The loading is easy to underrate because it starts small. At 2 %, on the cheapest exempt single policy in Victoria, it adds $25 a year. But it applies for ten years, and it grows with every 1 July you let pass. Those figures are on the cheapest policy available. On a policy three times the price, every figure triples. The rebate does not soften it, because the rebate is worked out on the premium without the loading. Below the surcharge threshold, the loading is the only stick For someone on $115,000, waiting also means the Medicare levy surcharge: $1,150 a year at the 2026-27 tier 1 rate, against $1,028 for the cheapest Victorian policy after the tier 1 rebate, so the surcharge is the dearer option even before the loading is counted. Below $105,000 there is no surcharge, and the decision rests on the loading and on what you want the cover for. A 31 year old at the base tier pays $930 a year for that policy after the 24.118 % rebate. Is private health insurance worth it weighs the two sides at each income. Three common mistakes The first is counting from the birthday instead of from the 1 July after it. Turning 31 does not start the loading; the following 1 July does, and that date can be almost a year away. The second is thinking that any policy will do. A policy with extras only, an insurance policy from another country, or Overseas Visitors Health Cover kept from before permanent residence does not count as hospital cover for the loading. The third is cancelling soon after the base day. Holding cover on the base day protects you, but a later gap counts against your lifetime allowance of 1,094 days, and once that is used a loading returns on rejoining. A fourth, less common, is believing that a loading is permanent. It is removed after ten years of continuous hospital cover, so a person who joins at 33 with a 6 % loading pays it until about 43 and then pays the same premium as everyone else. The ten year removal page counts down the months. Young people and the age-based discount Since 1 April 2019, insurers may offer people aged 18 to 29 a discount on hospital premiums: 2 % for each year under 30, up to 10 % for those who join between 18 and 25 ( PrivateHealth.gov.au ). The discount stays until 41, then falls by 2 % each year. It is the mirror image of the loading, but voluntary: an insurer can offer it on some products and not others, and a person covered as a dependant on a family policy cannot have it. Our premiums are the full prices of the file, before any such discount. Dependants on a parent's policy PrivateHealth.gov.au states that dependants who hold hospital cover on their base day avoid the loading. If you are still on your parents' policy on your base day, you meet the deadline; the question then is to take a policy of your own without a gap of more than your permitted days. The days of absence page explains the allowance. When the date moves Two groups have a different base day. New migrants have until the later of their usual base day and the first anniversary of their full Medicare registration ( new migrants ). Australian citizens and permanent residents who were overseas on their base day have until the first anniversary of their return ( returning from overseas ). Members of the ADF on continuous full-time service whose care is provided through the ADF, and people listed on a DVA Gold Card, are treated as holding hospital cover. The full rule is on the Lifetime Health Cover loading page . When exactly is my Lifetime Health Cover base day? For most people, the 1 July that follows the 31st birthday. A person who turns 31 on 2 July has almost a full year; one who turns 31 on 30 June has one day. Exceptions move the date for new migrants and for Australians who were overseas on that 1 July. The base day is never earlier than 1 July 2000, when the scheme began. I had cover on my 31st birthday but cancelled before 1 July. Is that enough? No. What counts is holding hospital cover on the base day itself. PrivateHealth.gov.au gives the case of Chloe, who turned 31 in January 2019, held cover on her birthday, cancelled in March and took out a new policy in September. Her base day was 1 July 2019, she had no cover on it, and she pays a 2 % loading. Does the loading start the day after my base day or a year later? At once. Join the day after your base day and you were 31 on the 1 July before joining, so the loading is 2 %. Each further 1 July without cover adds 2 %: someone who was 32 on the 1 July before joining pays 4 %, and someone who was 35 pays 10 %. The loading then stays fixed for the ten loaded years. Can I keep an age-based discount if I join before 30? Insurers may offer up to 10 % off hospital premiums to people who join between 18 and 29, 2 % for each year under 30. The discount is kept until 41, then reduced by 2 % a year. It is optional for the insurer, and dependants on a family policy cannot receive it.

mls-125000.text: At $125,000 a single person has just crossed into tier 2. The calculator shows the surcharge, the smaller rebate and the cheapest policy that removes both questions. A single income for MLS purposes of $125,000 in 2026-27 is $2,000 above the tier 1 ceiling of $123,000, so it falls in tier 2. The surcharge rate there is 1.25 %, charged on the whole of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, not just on the part above the line: $1,563 for a full year without hospital cover. That design creates a jump. At $123,000 the surcharge is $1,230; one dollar more and it is $1,538, $308 extra for a single dollar of income. The rebate steps down at the same point, from 16.079 % to 8.038 % for people under 65, so the cheapest policy becomes dearer exactly when the surcharge rises. In Victoria the cheapest exempt single policy costs $1,127 a year after the tier 2 rebate, $436 less than the surcharge at this income. The tier boundary in dollars Look at the two middle rows. Between $123,000 and $123,001 the surcharge rises by $308 and the net price of the cheapest Victorian policy rises by $99, because the rebate falls. Somebody hovering around the line who holds no cover is better off with the policy on either side of it, and the gap widens in tier 2. What sits inside $125,000 The tier is set by income for MLS purposes, which is broader than taxable income: it adds reportable fringe benefits, reportable super contributions and net investment losses. The rate is then charged on a narrower base, taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits. A person with $110,000 of taxable income and $15,000 of salary sacrificed into super has $125,000 for the tier but is charged on $110,000: $1,375 instead of $1,563. The ATO's own example of Josh follows the same logic. The super and investment losses page goes further. If your income moved during the year The tier is decided on the income of the whole year, known only when you lodge. A bonus paid in June can lift a year spent in tier 1 into tier 2 after the fact, for the surcharge and for the rebate alike. If you hold a policy and take the rebate as a premium reduction, tell your insurer your expected tier; the ATO warns that claiming too much as a premium reduction may leave a tax liability. If you hold no policy, every day of cover from now on removes a day of surcharge; the part-year page does that sum. How much loading the comparison can carry A late joiner pays a Lifetime Health Cover loading on top of the premium, with no rebate on it. At $125,000 the surcharge leaves room for quite a lot. On the cheapest NSW single policy, $1,231 a year before the rebate, cover stays cheaper than the $1,563 surcharge up to a loading of about 35 %, which is what someone first joining at about 47 would carry. Beyond that the surcharge is cheaper for the ten loaded years, and the choice turns on what happens after them. The loading page gives the percentage for your age. Across the states at $125,000 The surcharge is a federal tax and is the same in every state, $1,563. The policy is not. In Western Australia the cheapest exempt single policy costs $870 a year after the tier 2 rebate, leaving a margin of $692; in the Northern Territory it is $434. Residents of the ACT buy New South Wales policies. The comparison page ranks every state for any hospital tier. Neighbouring incomes At $110,000 the surcharge is the 1 % of tier 1 and the margin over the cheapest policy is thin; see the $110,000 page . At $150,000 you are deep in tier 2, where the surcharge has grown but the rebate has not moved; see the $150,000 page . Why does the surcharge jump at $123,001? Because each tier's rate applies to the whole surcharge base, not only to the slice above the threshold. At $123,000 you pay 1 %, $1,230; at $123,001 you pay 1.25 % on everything, $1,538. Income tax brackets work the other way, on the slice only, which is why the surcharge surprises people. How much rebate is lost by moving from tier 1 to tier 2? For a person under 65 the rate falls from 16.079 % to 8.038 %, about half. On a hospital policy costing $2,000 a year before the rebate, that is about $161 more to pay. Older households lose the same number of points: 24.118 % to 16.079 % at 70 or over. Can salary packaging lower the surcharge at $125,000? It does not lower the tier, since reportable fringe benefits count in income for MLS purposes and are part of the surcharge base. Super contributions are different: they count for the tier but the rate is not charged on them. With $15,000 of salary sacrificed into super, the surcharge falls to $1,375, though you stay in tier 2.

private-health-insurance.text: New to the subject? Enter your income and state: the calculator shows what the tax system charges you without hospital cover and what the cheapest policy costs with it. Private health insurance in Australia comes in two parts that the tax system treats very differently. Hospital cover pays towards treatment as a private patient in hospital; general treatment cover, often called extras, pays towards dental, optical, physiotherapy and similar services; some policies add ambulance. Only hospital cover takes you out of the Medicare levy surcharge, the extra 1 % to 1.5 % that a single person with an income for MLS purposes over $105,000 pays in 2026-27 without it. The government rebate, by contrast, applies to hospital, general treatment and ambulance policies alike, from 24.118 % of the premium for most people under 65 down to nothing at the top income tier. The Lifetime Health Cover loading, finally, is added by your insurer if you first buy hospital cover after the 1 July following your 31st birthday. Those three rules, the surcharge, the rebate and the loading, are the whole tax side of private health insurance. Three products, one tax rule that matters An Australian health insurer sells hospital cover, general treatment cover and ambulance cover, alone or combined. Since 1 April 2020 every hospital policy has been classified in one of four tiers, Gold, Silver, Bronze or Basic, with Plus versions of the lower three for policies that cover more than the minimum. The tier tells you what a policy must cover; it tells the tax office nothing. For the surcharge, the only question is whether you hold hospital cover from a registered Australian insurer with an excess of no more than $750 on a policy for one person or $1,500 on a couple or family policy. The surcharge: the cost of having no hospital cover The Medicare levy surcharge is charged by the ATO on your tax return, on top of the 2 % Medicare levy most taxpayers pay. It applies for each day of the income year on which you, your spouse or a dependent child had no appropriate hospital cover while your income for MLS purposes was over the threshold. In 2026-27 the rate is 1 % from $105,001 for a single person, 1.25 % from $123,001 and 1.5 % from $164,001. The thresholds page has the family figures, and income for MLS purposes explains why that income is larger than your taxable income. A Victorian aged 29 on $118,000 pays $1,180 of surcharge without cover. The cheapest exempt single policy in Victoria costs $102.10 a month before the rebate, $1,028 a year after it, so the policy is $152 cheaper than the tax. The rebate: a government discount on the premium You can take the rebate as reduced premiums throughout the year, the insurer applying the percentage you nominate, or pay the full premium and receive a refundable tax offset when you lodge your return. Either way, the percentage depends on two things, the income tier of the policy holder (the same tiers as the surcharge) and the age of the oldest person on the policy. The ATO warns that if you claim too much rebate as a premium reduction, for instance because your income moved into a higher tier, you may have a tax liability when you lodge. The rebate page has the full table and premium reduction or tax offset compares the two ways of claiming. The loading: the price of joining late If you buy hospital cover for the first time after your Lifetime Health Cover base day, normally the 1 July after your 31st birthday, the insurer adds 2 % to the hospital premium for each year you were over 30 on the 1 July before joining, up to 70 %, for 10 continuous years. The rebate is not paid on that extra. New migrants and Australians returning from overseas have their own deadlines. The loading page prices it on the cheapest policy of your state. The calendar of a policy holder Three dates organise the year. On 1 April insurers apply their new premiums and the rebate percentages are adjusted: in 2026 the average rise was 4.41 % and the rebate factor 0.993. On 1 July the surcharge and rebate thresholds move with the new income year. Between July and October most people lodge their return, where question M2 settles the surcharge with the help of the private health insurance statement your insurer sends. A couple policy in Queensland, for instance, starts at $205.98 a month before the rebate in the file of 1 October 2026; that figure will change on 1 April 2027. What to decide, and where to go next If your income is under the threshold, private cover is a health and budget choice with no tax at stake, apart from the loading that builds up after 31. If it is over, the cheapest exempt policy is almost always cheaper than the surcharge, and the question becomes how much more you are willing to pay for cover you would use. Is private health insurance worth it finds your break-even income, compare health insurance reads the whole policy file for your state, and basic hospital cover looks at the cheapest tier in detail. Do I have to buy private health insurance in Australia? No. Medicare covers residents as public patients and nobody is obliged to hold a private policy. The law only adds a cost if you do not: the Medicare levy surcharge when your income for MLS purposes is over $105,000 single or $210,000 family in 2026-27, and the Lifetime Health Cover loading if you take hospital cover late. Which kinds of policy get the government rebate? PrivateHealth.gov.au says the rebate applies to hospital, general treatment and ambulance policies provided by Australian registered health insurers. It does not apply to Overseas Visitors Health Cover or to other types of insurance such as travel insurance. The percentage depends on your income tier and on the age of the oldest person on the policy. What is the age-based discount for people under 30? Since 1 April 2019 insurers may offer people aged 18 to 29 a discount on hospital premiums of 2 % for each year under 30, up to 10 % for ages 18 to 25. The discount is kept until 41, then phased out by 2 % a year. It is optional for the insurer, and our premiums do not include it. Can adult children stay on a family policy? The law lets insurers cover single dependants aged 18 to 31, and dependants with a disability without an age limit, but each insurer chooses its own age range. For the surcharge, a person covered as a dependant on a family hospital policy is not liable as long as they have no spouse or dependants of their own. When do the figures for private health insurance change? Twice a year. Premiums and rebate percentages change on 1 April; the 2026-27 rebate rates run to 31 March 2027. Income thresholds for the surcharge and the rebate change on 1 July with the income year. Your tax return then settles both: the surcharge at question M2 and any rebate not already taken as a premium reduction.

rebate-over-65.text: Enter the age of the oldest person on your policy, your premium and your income: you see your rebate now and what the proposed 1 April 2027 change would take off it. People aged 65 and over receive a higher private health insurance rebate than younger people on the same income. Until 31 March 2027, when the oldest person on the policy is 65 to 69, the rebate is 28.139 % at the base tier, 20.098 % at tier 1 and 12.058 % at tier 2; from 70 it is 32.158 %, 24.118 % and 16.079 %. Under 65, the same tiers give 24.118 %, 16.079 % and 8.038 %. In July 2026 the Department of Health announced that from 1 April 2027 everyone would receive the under-65 rates, "subject to legislation passing Parliament", and put the average extra cost for those affected at $252 a year. The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives on 15 October 2026. On 19 October 2026 it is still before the house of representatives: it is not law, and the rates you pay today are unchanged. Today's extra support, row by row The rebate has three rows. A policy whose oldest member is under 65 sits on the first; 65 to 69, the second; 70 and over, the third. On the same income, the second row adds about four points and the third about eight, at every tier except tier 3, which receives no rebate at any age. The tiers for 2026-27 are the surcharge tiers: base tier up to $105,000 for a single person and $210,000 for a couple. Many retirees sit at the base tier because their income for surcharge purposes is low, even when their assets are not, and that is where the extra support is largest in dollars. What the bill would do The Department of Health paper of July 2026 says that from 1 April 2027 older Australians "will receive the same rebate rate as other people in the same income tier, subject to legislation passing Parliament". Its reasons: people on the same income currently receive different support depending on age, and the savings would go to aged care, including residential places and home care. It estimates the average extra cost for the people affected at $252 a year, "less than a dollar a day". The vehicle is the Private Health Insurance Amendment (Modernising the Private Health Insurance Rebate) Bill 2026 [No. 2] . The Parliament site records its introduction and the moving of the second reading in the House of Representatives on 15 October 2026, and gives its status as before the House. A bill needs to pass both chambers and receive assent before it changes anything. Until then this page treats the 2027 rates as a scenario. What is certain and what is not Certain: the rates in the first three columns apply until 31 March 2027. Not certain: whether the bill passes, in this form or amended, and when. Also not known yet: the rates for under 65s from 1 April 2027. The department says the adjustment factor would be 1 that year, but the ATO will only publish the 1 April 2027 rates in March 2027. The cost for typical retired households The department's average hides a wide range. The loss is the gap between your row and the first row, applied to your full premium. A large Gold policy loses more dollars than a Basic one; a household at tier 2 loses about the same number of points as one at the base tier, but on a smaller rebate. Premiums themselves will also move on 1 April 2027, as they do every year (the average increase was 4.41 % in 2026). The figures above isolate the effect of the rebate change alone. Couples with an age gap The age band is not a personal attribute: it belongs to the policy, and it is set by its oldest member. A couple aged 62 and 66 today receives the 65 to 69 row on the whole premium, 28.139 % at the base tier, so the younger partner benefits from the older one's age. That also means the proposed change would reach households where only one person is over 65. On the median NSW couple policy, such a couple at the base tier would lose $178 a year. A couple who both stay under 65 until after April 2027 would see no change at all, whatever happens to the bill. Income works the same way for everyone. The tier comes from the income for surcharge purposes of both partners together, tested on the family thresholds when you have a spouse on 30 June. A retired couple whose combined income for surcharge purposes stays under the family threshold sits at the base tier, where both the current extra support and the proposed loss are largest. Should anything change now? For most people, no. The proposal does not change what any policy covers, and dropping hospital cover has its own cost: a Lifetime Health Cover loading may apply if you return later, and the surcharge applies to incomes above the threshold. The department paper points to the Ombudsman's comparison service at PrivateHealth.gov.au for anyone who wants to look at cheaper cover, and notes that switching usually does not mean serving waiting periods again for services your current policy already covers. Compare health insurance shows how the cheapest policies differ by state. The general rule for the rebate is on the rebate page . Is the rebate for over 65s being cut in 2027? It is proposed, not decided. The Department of Health says older Australians would receive the same rate as others in their income tier from 1 April 2027, subject to legislation. The Modernising the Private Health Insurance Rebate Bill 2026 [No. 2] was introduced on 15 October 2026 and is before the house of representatives as of 19 October 2026. We will update this page when it passes or fails. How much more would a retired couple pay if the bill passes? On the median NSW couple policy that avoids the surcharge, $4,434 a year, a couple whose oldest member is 67 and whose income is at the base tier would lose $178 a year. If the oldest is 72, the loss is $356. The department's average for all affected people is $252. Would the 2027 rates still change with the rebate adjustment factor? Not on 1 April 2027. The department says the adjustment factor will be set to 1 for that date, so the under-65 percentages stay at 24.118 %, 16.079 % and 8.038 %. Indexation would resume on 1 April 2028, based on the gap between inflation and the average premium increase. Would people under 65 lose anything under the 2027 proposal? No. Under the department's table the under-65 row stays at 24.118 %, 16.079 % and 8.038 % on 1 April 2027, the same as today, because the adjustment factor would be set to 1 that year. Only the 65 to 69 and 70 and over rows would come down to those figures. Tier 3 stays at zero for everyone. Does the proposed change affect the Medicare levy surcharge? No. The bill concerns the rebate percentages only. The surcharge thresholds for 2026-27 ($105,000 single and $210,000 for couples and families) and its rates of 1 % to 1.5 % are unchanged, and so is the Lifetime Health Cover loading.

state-vic.text: The surcharge you avoid is a fixed sum for your income. Here is how far it goes at each hospital tier in Victoria. A single Victorian on $135,000 of income for MLS purposes is in tier 2 for 2026-27 and would pay $1,688 of Medicare levy surcharge without hospital cover. The cheapest open policy that avoids it costs $102.10 a month before the rebate in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, so $1,127 a year after the 8.038 % rebate. That leaves $561 of the surcharge unspent, and the question becomes how much better a policy that money buys. The cheapest Bronze Plus policy costs $1,412 net, the cheapest Silver Plus $1,848 and the cheapest Gold $2,743. The table below gives each tier at its cheapest and at its median price, and the full calculator above takes your own income and premium. The ladder from Basic to Gold Read the fourth column as the extra you would pay, or keep, compared with paying the surcharge and holding no cover. At this income the four lower rungs, Basic to Bronze Plus, cost less than the tax at their cheapest. Silver and Silver Plus cost a few hundred dollars more, and Gold over a thousand more; the median Gold policy at $418.25 a month costs about 1.7 times its cheapest one. The cheapest Gold single policy in the state comes from Mildura Health Fund. Where the money goes at other incomes The same ladder looks different on either side of $135,000. Just over the threshold, at $106,000, the surcharge is only $1,060 while the rebate is higher, 16.079 %, so the cheapest policy costs $1,028 and the margin above it is thin. In tier 3, at $180,000, the surcharge reaches $2,700 and there is no rebate at all: the cheapest Gold policy then costs $2,983, more than the surcharge. The page for $170,000 looks at the top tier in detail. A loading changes every row. The Lifetime Health Cover loading is a percentage added to the hospital premium, and it is the same percentage on a Basic as on a Gold policy, so in dollars it is three times larger on Gold. Someone joining at 45 with a 30 % loading would add $895 a year to the cheapest Gold policy and $368 to the cheapest Basic one. See the loading page . How to use the ladder Start from the surcharge you would pay, since it is money you spend either way once you are over the threshold. Subtract the net cost of the cheapest policy: what is left is the budget for better cover that costs you nothing extra compared with doing nothing. At $135,000 that budget is $561 a year, about $47 a month, enough to reach the cheapest Bronze Plus policy in the table with room to spare. Beyond that, each step up is paid for by you, not by the tax you avoid. Two cautions apply. A tier name sets the floor of what a policy covers, so read the Private Health Information Statement of each candidate. And waiting periods, which the Ombudsman warns may apply again after a break in cover, are not modelled here. Couples and families in Victoria For two people the cheapest exempt policy is $204.20 a month and the cheapest Gold $497.10; for a family, $204.20 and $497.10. Their surcharge is tested on the combined income against the family threshold, so the ladder above applies with the household sum in place of a single income. Sources: PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 ( data.gov.au ); tiers: PrivateHealth.gov.au ; thresholds and rebate: ATO . Naming a policy reports a price, not a recommendation. How the figures are built . Which hospital tier can I get in Victoria for the price of the surcharge? At $135,000 the surcharge is $1,688. Every tier whose cheapest Victorian policy costs less than that after the rebate is affordable for the same money: Basic, Basic Plus, Bronze, Bronze Plus. The answer moves with your income, since both the surcharge and the rebate depend on it. Why is Silver Plus sometimes cheaper than Silver in Victoria? Because tier names set a minimum list of covered treatments, not a price. Victoria has 203 open Silver Plus single policies and only 16 plain Silver ones, so the cheapest Silver Plus at $167.45 undercuts the cheapest Silver at $179.35 a month. Compare policies across tiers, not only within one. How many hospital policies avoid the surcharge in Victoria? 455 open single policies from 22 insurers, 454 couple policies and 861 family policies in the file of 1 October 2026. Each excess option of a product is counted as a policy. Restricted funds, corporate products and policies with an excess above the limits are left out.

compare-health-insurance.text: Choose a household and the lowest hospital tier you would accept: the table ranks every state by its cheapest open policy that avoids the surcharge. Comparing health insurance in Australia does not require a quote form. The Private Health Insurance Ombudsman publishes every policy on sale, with its premium in each state, its hospital tier and its excess, and releases the whole file each month on data.gov.au. In the release of 1 October 2026 we count 455 open single policies in Victoria that avoid the Medicare levy surcharge, sold by 22 insurers, and 3,129 such state and policy combinations across the country. Inside one state and one tier the spread is wide: a Victorian single Gold policy costs from $248.55 a month before the rebate, while the median Gold policy costs $418.25. Comparison sites show the policies of insurers they have agreements with. The table on this page shows the cheapest of all of them, for each state and tier, and stops there. It is a starting point for your own reading of each policy statement, not a recommendation of any insurer. What the public file contains The Ombudsman publishes the details of every policy on sale on PrivateHealth.gov.au and, in bulk, on data.gov.au . For each policy the file gives the insurer, the policy name, the states where it is sold, the kind of cover (single, couple, single parent, family), the hospital tier, the excess and the monthly premium. That is enough to answer the one question most comparison services avoid putting in a table: what is the cheapest policy that does a given job, in a given state, for a given household? We apply three filters. We keep hospital and combined policies with an excess of no more than $750 per person and $1,500 per policy, because only those avoid the surcharge. We drop the 9 restricted funds, corporate products and policies sold only together with another one, because most readers cannot buy them. And we keep the rest, every insurer, with no ranking by commission. The method page gives the counts at each step. Victoria, single cover: the spread inside each tier Two patterns come out of the table. The first is that the tier is not a price band: some Plus policies of a lower tier cost more than the cheapest policy of the tier above, because Plus policies add categories of treatment beyond the minimum. The second is that the gap between the cheapest and the median policy grows as you move up. At the Basic tier the median is 11 % above the cheapest; at Gold it is 68 % above. Two Gold policies are not the same product, since they differ in the hospitals the insurer has agreements with, the extras bundled with them and the gap arrangements, none of which the file prices. The same comparison for a family A family policy in Victoria starts at $204.20 a month before the rebate, with a median of $451.90 across 861 open policies. Family premiums are about twice single ones for the same policy, and the rebate is the same percentage, so the comparison with the surcharge depends on the combined income. A family whose income for MLS purposes is over $210,000 must cover both partners and every dependent child to avoid the surcharge; one person left out and the household pays it. The families page works through the thresholds with children. What a comparison should check, in order Does it remove the surcharge? Hospital cover, a registered Australian insurer, an excess within the limits. Extras only, Overseas Visitors Health Cover and foreign insurers do not count. What does it cover? Read the Private Health Information Statement. A Basic policy can cost less than half the price of a Gold one because it covers far less; the Basic cover page looks at what that means. What does it cost you? The full premium, minus your rebate percentage, plus your Lifetime Health Cover loading if you have one. The cover calculator on the home page does that sum with your own premium. How does it compare with not buying? Above the threshold, set that net cost against the surcharge. Below it, there is no tax at stake, and the only penalty for waiting is the loading that builds up after your base day. Why we name the cheapest policy and nothing else The surcharge comparison needs a price, and the honest price to use is the lowest one any reader could actually pay. So the calculators name the cheapest open policy of the file for each state and household, ahm health insurance at $102.10 for a Basic single policy in Victoria at the time of writing. Naming it is not an endorsement. We have no agreement with any insurer, receive no referral fee and do not collect your details, and the policy that is cheapest this month may not be next month: premiums change every 1 April and the file is republished every month. Check the date of the release at the foot of each table before you rely on a premium, and read the policy statement on PrivateHealth.gov.au before you buy anything. Where does the policy data on this page come from? From the PrivateHealth.gov.au product file that the Private Health Insurance Ombudsman publishes on data.gov.au under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia licence. We read the release of 1 October 2026, 31,864 product lines, and keep the hospital policies open to the public whose excess avoids the surcharge. The script that builds our table can be run again on each monthly release. Why are restricted funds left out of the comparison? Restricted funds only accept members of a given employer, profession or community, so most readers cannot buy their policies. The file lists 9 of them.
