If you belong to one, ask it for its premium and type it into the cover calculator as your own premium: the comparison with the surcharge works the same way for any policy. How should two hospital policies in the same tier be compared? Start with the Private Health Information Statement of each policy, which PrivateHealth.gov.au publishes in a standard format for every insurer. A tier only sets the minimum categories of treatment; Plus policies cover more. Then compare the excess, which must stay within the surcharge limits, and finally the premium after your own rebate percentage. Do the premiums here include the rebate or any discount? No. They are the full monthly premiums of the file, before the government rebate and before any age-based discount an insurer may give people under 30. Your own price is lower by the rebate of your tier, 24.118 % at the base tier for most people under 65, and higher by any Lifetime Health Cover loading.

lhc-new-migrants.text: Arrived recently and over 31? Enter your age on the 1 July before you would join: if your twelve months have passed, the calculator gives your loading and its price in your state. A new migrant to Australia gets a base day of their own for Lifetime Health Cover: the later of the 1 July following the 31st birthday and the first anniversary of full Medicare registration. In practice, someone who arrives at 38 and registers for Medicare has twelve months from that registration to take out private hospital cover with no loading. Full registration means registration for interim or full Medicare benefits, usually shown by a blue or green Medicare card; reciprocal Medicare does not count. Miss the twelve months and the normal rule applies: 2 % for every year you were over 30 on the 1 July before joining. PrivateHealth.gov.au gives the case of Sonja, registered in April 2013 and insured only in October 2018 at 36: her loading is 12 %. On the cheapest single policy in Western Australia, $946 a year, that is $114 more each year for ten years. Two dates, take the later one For anyone who arrives in Australia already over 31, the usual deadline has long passed. The rules give them a fresh one. PrivateHealth.gov.au sets the base day of a new migrant at the later of: the 1 July following the 31st birthday; or the first anniversary of full Medicare registration. The ATO says the same thing in its list of people who do not pay the loading: a new migrant aged 31 or over who had hospital cover within 12 months of being registered for full Medicare benefits. For a migrant who arrives at 27, the first date is the later one and the usual rule applies. For a migrant who arrives at 45, it is the anniversary of registration. Sonja's case, step by step The Ombudsman's example shows the order of the tests. Sonja registers for full Medicare benefits, a green card, on 20 April 2013. Her 31st birthday is on 8 January 2014. The anniversary of her registration is 20 April 2014; the 1 July after her 31st birthday is 1 July 2014. The later of the two is 1 July 2014, so that is her base day. She buys private hospital cover on 2 October 2018, aged 36, and pays 12 %: (36 minus 30) times 2 %. Had she registered at 33 instead, her base day would have been the anniversary of registration, and any policy bought in the following twelve months would have carried no loading at all. A couple who arrived together When both partners miss the window, each has their own loading, and the couple policy carries the average. A couple aged 42 and 39 on the 1 July before joining have 24 % and 18 %, so 21 % on the policy. On the cheapest couple policy in Western Australia, $1,893 a year before the rebate, that adds $397 a year for ten years. If one partner joined within the window and the other did not, the average halves the late joiner's loading. Choosing a policy inside the window Any private hospital policy from an Australian registered insurer meets the Lifetime Health Cover deadline, whatever its tier. A migrant who wants time to compare can take a low cost Basic policy before the anniversary, keep it, and move to a fuller policy later: changing product or insurer without a gap does not reset anything, and the loading stays at zero. The cheapest single policy in Western Australia that also avoids the surcharge costs $78.86 a month before the rebate in the file of 1 October 2026; the Western Australia page lists the others. Visitors, students and the policies that do not count Many people arrive on a temporary visa that requires Overseas Visitors Health Cover or Overseas Student Health Cover. Neither counts as hospital cover for Lifetime Health Cover, and neither stops the Medicare levy surcharge either. Before full Medicare registration, the Lifetime Health Cover window has not opened. Once a visa holder is registered for full or interim Medicare benefits, the twelve months run, and a visitor policy kept out of habit does not stop them running. The documents your insurer may ask for A Medicare registration date letter , obtained from Services Australia, to show when your twelve months began. An International Movement Record from the Department of Home Affairs if you were overseas on the anniversary of your registration (for registrations from 1 July 2009). A clearance certificate from any previous Australian insurer, which a former insurer must provide within 14 days. Give them on or after joining so that your loading is reassessed. The Medicare levy surcharge is a separate clock The twelve month window concerns the loading only. The surcharge runs from the first day you are both liable and without hospital cover: once your income for MLS purposes is over $105,000 (single, 2026-27) and you are no longer in a Medicare levy exemption category, every day without an Australian hospital policy counts. A new resident on $140,000, liable for the surcharge from registration, who waits the full twelve months pays $1,750 in surcharge for a full year. Visa holders and expats sets out when the exemption ends. The general rule for everyone else is on the Lifetime Health Cover loading page , and the case of Australians coming home is on returning from overseas . When does the twelve month window for new migrants start? On the date you registered for interim or full Medicare benefits, the date usually tied to a blue or green Medicare card. Your base day is the first anniversary of that date, unless the 1 July after your 31st birthday is later. You can confirm the registration date by asking Services Australia for a Medicare registration date letter. Does reciprocal Medicare count as registration for Lifetime Health Cover? No. PrivateHealth.gov.au states that reciprocal Medicare does not count for Lifetime Health Cover purposes. The window opens only with registration for interim or full Medicare benefits. If you are unsure which date applies to you, the Medicare registration date letter settles it, and your insurer uses it to set your loading. Does Overseas Visitors Health Cover protect me from the loading? No. Overseas Visitors Health Cover, Overseas Student Health Cover and insurance from another country are not hospital cover for Lifetime Health Cover. Only private hospital cover from an Australian registered insurer counts. A visa holder who keeps a visitor policy after full Medicare registration still needs an Australian hospital policy within the twelve months. What do I give my insurer to avoid a loading as a new migrant? A letter from Medicare stating your registration date, supplied on or after joining, so that the insurer can reassess your loading. If you registered on or after 1 July 2009 and were overseas on the anniversary of your registration, you may also need an International Movement Record from the Department of Home Affairs. What if I left Australia soon after registering for Medicare? If you registered on or after 1 July 2009 and were overseas on the anniversary, you have twelve months from your first return to Australia for 90 days or more. PrivateHealth.gov.au describes Deepak, who registered in 2009, worked in France for six years with short visits home and returned in December 2015: his new base day was the anniversary of that return.

mls-150000.text: At $150,000 the tier is settled. The calculator shows the surcharge and the cheapest policy; open the options to remove super contributions or investment losses from the surcharge base. A single income for MLS purposes of $150,000 in 2026-27 sits in the middle of tier 2, which runs from $123,001 to $164,000. Without hospital cover for the full year, the surcharge is 1.25 % of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, $1,875 when the whole income is of that kind. How the income is made up matters here more than anywhere. Fringe benefits from salary packaging count in full, both for the tier and for the base. Super contributions and net investment losses count for the tier only, so the surcharge on the same $150,000 can be several hundred dollars lower. With the tier 2 rebate of 8.038 %, any hospital policy whose full premium is under about $169.91 a month costs less than the full surcharge, and the cheapest exempt single policies in every state are well under that line. Same $150,000, different surcharge The ATO defines income for MLS purposes as taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits, reportable super contributions, net investment losses and any amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid. That total picks the tier. The rate is then charged on taxable income, reportable fringe benefits and those trust amounts only. The rows above follow that rule: packaged benefits change nothing compared with salary, while super contributions and investment losses keep you in tier 2 but shrink the base. The salary packaging page goes through the income statement figures line by line. The premium ceiling at this income Turn the question around: how expensive can a hospital policy be before the surcharge is the cheaper option? For a single person under 65 with no loading, the answer is a full premium of about $169.91 a month. In New South Wales the median exempt policy of the Basic, Basic Plus, Bronze, Bronze Plus tiers costs less than that, while the median Gold single policy, $375.20, is far above it. In other words, at $150,000 the tax side pays for a mid-range policy, not for a top one. That ceiling falls when the surcharge base is smaller. With $25,000 of the income in super contributions and losses, as in the last row of the table, the surcharge is $1,563 and so is the most a policy can cost after the rebate and still win. The ceiling moves with age and loading Two forces pull the ceiling in opposite directions. Age raises it, because the rebate at tier 2 is 12.058 % from 65 and 16.079 % from 70, against 8.038 % below 65. A Lifetime Health Cover loading lowers it, because the loading is added to the full premium and the rebate is never paid on it. Someone who first takes out hospital cover at 50, with a 40 % loading, can only pay about $118.41 a month before the policy costs more than the surcharge. The cheapest exempt policies of the October file are still below that line in every state, but the choice of policy narrows quickly. The loading stops after ten continuous years of cover; the surcharge does not stop as long as your income stays above the threshold and you stay uncovered. Before you cross into tier 3 You are $14,001 from tier 3. There the surcharge rate rises to 1.5 % and the rebate disappears at every age, so the full premium becomes your price. The $170,000 page shows what that does to the comparison. Back at the start of tier 2, the $125,000 page explains the jump at $123,001. Thresholds move every 1 July, so an income that stays at $150,000 drifts slowly away from the next tier as the years pass. Do salary packaged benefits count for the surcharge? Yes, twice. Reportable fringe benefits, the grossed-up amount shown on your income statement, are part of income for MLS purposes, which sets the tier, and part of the base the rate is charged on. So $20,000 of packaged benefits on top of $130,000 of salary gives the same $1,875 surcharge as $150,000 of plain salary. What is the most I can pay for cover and still beat the surcharge on $150,000? About $169.91 a month before the rebate for a single person under 65 with no loading: at that premium the tier 2 rebate of 8.038 % brings the yearly cost to the $1,875 surcharge. In NSW the median exempt single policy costs $186.10. A loading lowers that ceiling. How far is $150,000 from the top surcharge tier? $14,001. From $164,001 the rate becomes 1.5 %, the surcharge $2,460 on a full year, and the rebate stops entirely at any age. A pay rise or bonus that crosses that line raises the surcharge and the net price of any policy you already hold.

mls-couples.text: Enter both incomes for MLS purposes: the tool finds the household tier, then shows what each partner would pay without hospital cover. A couple, married or de facto, with or without children, is tested on the family threshold: for 2026-27 the surcharge starts when the two partners' incomes for MLS purposes add up to more than $210,000. The combined total also decides the rate, 1 % up to $246,000, 1.25 % up to $328,000 and 1.5 % beyond. Each partner then pays that rate on their own taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, not on the household total, so the bill is split in proportion to income. A couple on $180,000 and $75,000, without cover, pays $2,250 and $938. A partner who had a spouse all year and whose own income for MLS purposes is $28,011 or less pays nothing (2025-26 figure, the latest published). To avoid the surcharge, both partners and every dependant need an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover, ideally on the same couple or family policy. How the household test works The ATO runs the test in two steps. First it adds your income for MLS purposes to your spouse's and compares the sum with the family thresholds. That gives the tier and the rate for the household. Then it charges each partner the rate on their own taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, for their own days without cover. The order matters: a high earner with a low-earning partner can end up below the family threshold and pay nothing, while a pair of middle incomes can cross it together. The household total is the same in every row, so the rate is the same. Only the split differs. The last row shows the spouse floor at work: the partner on $28,011 is not liable, and the other partner pays on their own income only. Who counts as your spouse For MLS purposes your spouse is a person of any sex who is legally married to you, whose relationship with you is registered under a prescribed state or territory law, or who lives with you on a genuine domestic basis as a couple. The ATO treats a spouse as your dependant regardless of their income: if your spouse worked at any time in the year and you had a spouse all year, you are still taken to have maintained them for the whole year. A temporary separation, for a holiday or travel overseas, does not end it. An ex-spouse to whom you pay maintenance is not your dependant. The year you move in, marry or separate When a couple forms or ends during the year, the M2 instructions split the year into periods. For the days you were single, you are liable if your own income for MLS purposes is over the single threshold and you lacked cover. For the days you had a spouse, you are liable only if your own income for MLS purposes is over the family threshold. The rate is set by your status on 30 June. The ATO gives two 2025-26 examples, with that year's thresholds of $101,000 and $202,000. Michael and Michelle separated on 12 October 2025. For the first 104 days each is compared with the family threshold, and neither is liable. For the 262 single days, Michelle's $102,000 is above $101,000; Michael's $69,000 is not. Michelle, single on 30 June, pays the tier 1 rate on her own income for those days: $732.16. Michael pays nothing. Alice and Adam married on 17 January 2026. For the first 200 days each is single; Alice's $150,000 is above the single threshold, Adam's $89,000 is not. After the wedding each is compared with the family threshold, and neither is over it. Because Alice is married on 30 June, her rate comes from the couple's combined $239,000, which was tier 2 in 2025-26: 1.25 % on her $142,000 of taxable income for 200 days, $972.60. If your spouse died during the year and you had no new spouse by 30 June, the ATO asks you to assume you had a spouse for the whole year when working out your income for MLS purposes. One policy or two The law asks that every member of the family hold an appropriate level of hospital cover. Two single policies, each with an excess of $750 or less, meet the condition as well as one couple policy with an excess of $1,500 or less. In the October 2026 premium file a couple policy is, for the cheapest products, exactly twice the single price, so the choice is about cover and convenience more than tax. The excess page has the limits. Sharing the bill fairly Because each partner pays on their own income, the surcharge lands mostly on the higher earner, while a couple policy is usually paid from one account. In the example of the summary, the household would pay $3,188 without cover, $2,250 of it on the $180,000 income. Compare that total with the net price of a couple policy in your state: the calculator on the home page does it with the rebate and any Lifetime Health Cover loading, which on a couple policy is the average of the two partners' loadings. Sources The two-step test, the floor and the change-of-status rules are in ATO, M2 Medicare levy surcharge 2026 (tax return instructions) ; the definition of a spouse and of maintenance in ATO, Family and dependants for Medicare levy surcharge purposes ; the thresholds in ATO, Medicare levy surcharge income, thresholds and rates (updated 22 June 2026) . PrivateHealth.gov.au confirms that couples are on the family tiers and that every member must be covered. Do de facto partners count as a couple for the surcharge? Yes. For MLS purposes your spouse includes a person of any sex you live with on a genuine domestic basis as a couple, and a person whose relationship with you is registered under a prescribed state or territory law. Marriage is not needed. Once you are a couple, the family threshold applies and your incomes for MLS purposes are combined. If only one partner has hospital cover, does the couple avoid the surcharge? No. Above the family threshold, the surcharge applies for any day on which you, your spouse or a dependent child lacked an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. PrivateHealth.gov.au says it plainly: if your partner or one of your dependants is not covered, you pay. A single policy in one name leaves both partners exposed. Does a low-earning partner pay the surcharge? Not if their own income for MLS purposes is $28,011 or less and they had a spouse for the whole year. The M2 instructions for 2025-26 give that figure; the ATO page on paying the surcharge, last updated in May 2026, still prints an older, lower amount. The 2026-27 amount had not been published on 19 October 2026. The higher earner still pays on their own income. What happens to the surcharge in the year we marry or separate? Both thresholds can apply, each for its own period. For the days you were single you are compared with the single threshold, for the days you had a spouse with the family one, using your own income for MLS purposes in each test. The rate is then set by your situation on 30 June: combined income and family tiers with a spouse, own income and single tiers without. Does our surcharge change if my spouse earns nothing? The test then rests on your income alone against the family threshold of $210,000, which is twice the single one. A spouse with no income is still your dependant, and still needs hospital cover. On $180,000 with a spouse earning nothing you pay no surcharge at all; single, the same income would cost $2,700 without cover.

rebate-premium-reduction-or-tax-offset.text: Choose the tier you would nominate and test the income you really expect: the calculator shows the rebate you are owed, so you can see whether a tax bill or a refund is coming. The private health insurance rebate can reach you in two ways, and the amount is the same in the end. Most people take it as a premium reduction: you nominate an income tier with your insurer, which charges you the premium minus the rebate of that tier. The alternative is to pay the full premium and claim the rebate as a refundable tax offset when you lodge your return. Either way, the ATO checks your actual income for surcharge purposes after 30 June. If you nominated a tier that was too low, you received too much rebate and the difference becomes a tax liability; if you nominated too high a tier, the ATO pays the shortfall as an offset. There is no extra penalty for a wrong estimate. In 2026-27 the tiers moved up: the base tier for a single person now runs to $105,000 instead of $101,000, so some people who nominated tier 1 last year can now nominate the base tier and pay less each month. Same entitlement, different timing The rebate you are owed for a year is fixed after 30 June, once your income for surcharge purposes and your family status on that day are known. What you choose is only how the money moves before then. Both are described on the ATO eligibility page and on PrivateHealth.gov.au . The rebate itself is the same percentage either way: 24.118 %, 16.079 % or 8.038 % under 65, more when the oldest person covered is 65 or over. The cost of nominating the wrong tier Suppose your full premium is $3,000 a year and everyone on the policy is under 65. Every step between the tier you nominate and the tier you end up in is worth a fixed amount, which the table sets out. The amounts are modest, but they arrive in one go with the notice of assessment, and they come on top of any Medicare levy surcharge if the same income rise also took you above the surcharge threshold without hospital cover. Nominating a tier higher than you expect, or taking the rebate at tax time, removes the risk of a bill at the price of paying more during the year. The ATO example: a promotion in the middle of the year The ATO tells the story of Belinda, single, whose employer pays her hospital premium under a salary sacrifice arrangement. At the start of 2025-26 her income for surcharge purposes is $132,000, tier 2, and her employer pays premiums reduced by the tier 2 rebate. Part way through the year a promotion lifts her income to $159,000, which is tier 3 for that year (the 2025-26 tier 3 threshold was $158,001). She is not entitled to any rebate from that point, but she does not tell her insurer. When she lodges, she has a tax liability for the excess reduction she received. Two lessons come out of it: the employer paying the premium does not change whose income counts, and a pay rise is the moment to update your nominated tier. The 2026-27 thresholds move tiers down Income thresholds rise each 1 July. For 2026-27 the single tiers are $105,000, $123,000 and $164,000, up from $101,000, $118,000 and $158,000. An income that has not changed may therefore fall into a lower tier this year, with a higher rebate. A single person on $103,000 was at tier 1 in 2025-26 and is at the base tier in 2026-27; if they kept their old nomination, they are paying $241 a year too much on a $3,000 premium and will get it back only at tax time. PrivateHealth.gov.au also notes that the new rebate rates of 1 April 2026 applied to the old thresholds until 30 June 2026, so a return for 2025-26 uses two sets of rates. Several adults on one policy Each adult covered is a private health insurance incentive beneficiary and is income tested on their share. When a couple shares a policy, the rebate is spread evenly between them. A policy that covers only dependent children gives the entitlement to the parents, or, if they are not a couple on 30 June, to the one who pays the premiums. Changes of status during the year Because the tier is tested on your family status on 30 June, a change of status can make your nomination wrong even when your salary has not moved. Moving in with a partner before 30 June puts you on the family thresholds, tested on your combined income: $210,000 for the base tier in 2026-27. Separating and having no dependent child on 30 June puts you back on the single thresholds, tested on your own income. A single parent is always on the family thresholds with their own income alone. The ATO table of statuses covers the less common cases, such as the death of a spouse during the year, where the incomes of both are still used. When the change pushes you into a higher tier, the same reconciliation applies as for a pay rise: the excess rebate is collected when you lodge. When it pulls you into a lower one, the offset makes up the difference. Updating your tier with the insurer as soon as the change happens keeps both amounts small. Before you choose Look at the income you expect for the whole year, not your current salary: bonuses, reportable fringe benefits, salary sacrificed super and net investment losses all count. Income for MLS purposes adds them up. If you are near a threshold, the thresholds page shows what one more dollar changes for the surcharge and the rebate, and the rebate page gives the full table of rates. Is it better to take the rebate as a lower premium or at tax time? The total is the same, because the ATO reconciles both methods against your actual income after 30 June. A premium reduction spreads the benefit over the year and lowers each payment. Claiming it in your return means paying the full premium first and waiting for the refund. The premium reduction carries the risk of a tax bill if your income ends up in a higher tier than you nominated. What happens if I nominate the wrong income tier with my insurer? If your actual income is in a higher tier, you received more rebate than you were entitled to and you will have a tax liability for the excess when you lodge. If it is in a lower tier, the ATO gives you the missing amount as a tax offset. PrivateHealth.gov.au states there are no additional penalties for estimating your income incorrectly. How do I change the tier I nominated? Contact your insurer, or use the rebate claim form PrivateHealth.gov.au mentions, to nominate a new tier. The ATO advises telling your insurer when your income for surcharge purposes changes and you move into a different tier, so that the reduction you receive during the year stays close to what you will be entitled to. Who receives the rebate when an employer pays the premium? Each adult on the policy is income tested, whoever pays. If your employer pays your private health insurance, the ATO says you are generally entitled to the rebate as a reduced premium and your employer pays the rest. The tier is still set by your own income for surcharge purposes, as the ATO example of Belinda shows. Where does the rebate information on my tax return come from? Usually from your insurer. PrivateHealth.gov.au says rebate details are generally filled in automatically in the tax return, and you can ask your insurer for a statement after the end of the financial year. The statement shows the premiums paid, the rebate received as a reduction and the tier you nominated.

state-qld.text: Joining hospital cover late adds a loading to the premium but not to the surcharge. Enter your age to see where the balance tips in Queensland. The cheapest open hospital policy that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge in Queensland costs $102.99 a month for one person before the rebate, from see-u by HBF, in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026. For a single person who has held cover since their early thirties, it costs $1,161 a year after the rebate on an income of $125,000, against a surcharge of $1,563. Someone who first joins at 55 carries a Lifetime Health Cover loading of 50 %, charged on top of the premium and not covered by the rebate: the same policy then costs $1,754, more than the surcharge. The loading lasts ten years of continuous cover. This page gives, age by age, the net cost of the cheapest Queensland policy and the income from which it beats the surcharge. Age at joining against the surcharge The last column is the lowest income at which the cheapest policy, loading included, costs less than the surcharge. For someone covered since 31 it sits just above the $105,000 threshold. Each year of delay adds 2 % to the premium and pushes that income up, because the loading is paid in full while the rebate shrinks with income. The surcharge itself does not care when you were born. Why waiting rarely pays A loading is a ten-year cost, the surcharge a yearly one. Someone of 45 who stays uncovered for five more years on $125,000 pays the surcharge each of those years, then joins at 50 with 40 % instead of 30 %. On the cheapest Queensland policy at today's premium, those extra 10 % cost $124 a year for ten years. The base day page has a calculator for the cost of waiting, and the removal page counts the years left on a loading you already have. The rule that removes the loading is the same in every state: ten years of continuous hospital cover, with permitted gaps that do not break the count but do not add to it. A late joiner who keeps the cheapest policy for ten years and then moves up a tier pays the higher premium with no loading at all. A couple where one partner joins late Take a Brisbane couple: one partner has held hospital cover since their twenties, the other has never had any and is 47 on the 1 July before they join together. The late joiner's own loading is 34 %; averaged over the two adults, the couple policy carries 17 %. On the cheapest Queensland couple policy, $205.98 a month before the rebate, that average adds $420 a year. With incomes of $140,000 and $95,000, the couple would otherwise pay $2,350 of surcharge between them, and the cheapest couple policy with the averaged loading costs $2,495 after the rebate. The covered partner pays part of the price of the other's late start for as long as they share the policy, which is worth knowing before choosing between one couple policy and two single ones. Two single policies would cost $2,472 a year before the rebate, the loaded one carrying the full 34 %. The Queensland price list Families pay $205.98 a month for the cheapest exempt policy, couples $205.98 and single parents $158.25. On a couple or family policy the loading is the average of the two adults' loadings, so a partner who has held cover since 31 halves the loading of a late joiner. Sources: PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 ( data.gov.au ), Lifetime Health Cover rules , ATO thresholds . Naming a policy reports a price, not a recommendation. How the figures are built . Does a Lifetime Health Cover loading make the surcharge cheaper than cover? It can, at moderate incomes and late joining ages. In Queensland, at $125,000, the cheapest policy with a 60 % loading, the figure for joining at 60, costs $1,878 against a surcharge of $1,563. Paying the surcharge instead does not make the loading go away: it keeps rising each year you wait, up to 70 %. What is the cheapest exempt hospital policy in Queensland? In the file of 1 October 2026, "Starter Hospital $750 Excess with Daily Co-Pay (Basic)" from see-u by HBF, at $102.99 a month for one person before the rebate. The next two are GMHBA Limited at $105.50 and ahm health insurance at $106.15. This is a price from the public file, not a recommendation. Is hospital cover in Queensland dearer than in other states? For the cheapest policy, slightly: $102.99 a month is the highest of the seven price lists in the file, a little above New South Wales at $102.60 and Victoria at $102.10. Western Australia and the Northern Territory are much cheaper. The median policy in Queensland costs $193.75.

basic-hospital-cover.text: Choose your household and the lowest tier you would accept: the table shows, state by state, what that tier costs at its cheapest before the rebate. Basic is the lowest of the four tiers into which every Australian hospital policy has been classified since 1 April 2020, below Bronze, Silver and Gold. For the Medicare levy surcharge the tier does not matter: a Basic policy from a registered insurer with an excess of no more than $750 for one person or $1,500 for a couple or family is an appropriate level of hospital cover, exactly like a Gold one. That is why the cheapest policy that removes the surcharge is a Basic policy in every state in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026: from $39.30 a month for a single person in the Northern Territory to $102.99 in Queensland, before the rebate. The trade-off is cover. A tier sets the minimum categories of hospital treatment a policy must include, and Basic sets the fewest; several of the cheapest Basic policies carry the word "accident" in their name. In New South Wales the median Gold single policy costs 3.4 times the median Basic one. Four tiers, one test for the tax office Hospital policies have been sold in four tiers since the reform that became mandatory on 1 April 2020: Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic, with Plus versions of the lower three. PrivateHealth.gov.au explains that each tier is built on minimum standard clinical categories of treatment, such as "bone, joint and muscle" or "heart and vascular system", and that a policy covering a category must cover everything listed in it. Gold sets the longest list of categories; Basic the shortest. A Plus policy adds categories above the minimum of its tier. None of that changes the surcharge. The ATO asks whether you held private patient hospital cover with an excess within the limits on each day of the year; the tier is not part of the test. So for someone whose only aim is to stop paying the surcharge, Basic does the job at the lowest price. The cheapest Basic policy in each state The Northern Territory stands out, with Basic premiums well under half those of the eastern states. Western Australia comes next. Elsewhere the cheapest Basic single policy sits close to $100 a month. In 6 of the 7 regions the cheapest three Basic policies include one with "accident" in its name, which tells you what the insurer is selling: cover centred on treatment after an accident, plus the minimum the tier requires. What the low price buys, and what it does not A Basic policy removes the surcharge, counts as hospital cover for Lifetime Health Cover and receives the rebate. Those are its three tax effects, and above the threshold they often make it cheaper than paying the surcharge. A South Australian aged 33 on $120,000 pays $1,200 of surcharge without cover; even with the 6 % loading of a late start, the cheapest Basic policy costs $1,066 after the rebate. What it does not buy is broad hospital cover. If you need a hospital treatment outside the policy's categories, the policy pays no benefit for it, and the choice left is a public hospital under Medicare or paying as a private patient yourself. Before you choose Basic for the tax, read its Private Health Information Statement, which every insurer must send at least once a year and which PrivateHealth.gov.au publishes for every policy in a standard format. Compare it with a Bronze or Silver statement and decide whether the difference, in South Australia $72.69 a month between the cheapest Silver and the cheapest Basic single policy, is worth paying. Basic cover for a couple or a family The same logic applies to households, with one extra condition: to avoid the surcharge above the family threshold of $210,000, the policy must cover you, your partner and every dependent child. A family Basic policy costs about twice a single one; in New South Wales the cheapest starts at $205.20 a month before the rebate. Because both partners pay the surcharge on their own income once the household is over the line, a family on a combined income just above the threshold often finds that a family Basic policy costs less than the two surcharges together. The families page runs that comparison with children counted. The excess is the other trap Many of the cheapest hospital policies come with the highest excess the surcharge rules allow, often $750 for a single person. One with a higher excess may be cheaper still but does not avoid the surcharge: the limit is $750 for a single policy and $1,500 for a couple or family policy, for all claims in a year. The excess page checks your policy against those limits. Starting with Basic, moving up later A common path for people who join for tax reasons is to start on a Basic policy by their base day, avoid both the surcharge and the loading, and move to a higher tier when their needs change. Moving tier with the same or another insurer keeps your Lifetime Health Cover history, provided the cover is continuous. The turning 31 page has the deadline, and compare health insurance shows how the price climbs from tier to tier in each state. Does a Basic hospital policy really avoid the Medicare levy surcharge? Yes, provided it is hospital cover from a registered Australian insurer and its excess is within the limits: $750 a year on a policy for one person, $1,500 on a couple or family policy. The ATO and PrivateHealth.gov.au set no tier condition. Extras only cover and Overseas Visitors Health Cover do not count, whatever their price. What is the difference between Basic and Basic Plus? A Basic Plus policy covers everything a Basic policy must cover plus some extra categories of treatment chosen by the insurer. In NSW the cheapest Basic Plus single policy costs $111.60 a month against $102.60 for Basic. Which extra categories you get differs from one Plus policy to the next, so read the statement. Does Basic cover protect me from the Lifetime Health Cover loading? Yes. For Lifetime Health Cover, any private hospital cover with an Australian registered insurer counts, whatever its tier. Holding a Basic policy from your base day, and keeping it, means no loading when you later move to a higher tier, and switching tier or insurer does not restart the count. Extras only cover does not count. Is the rebate paid on Basic hospital cover? Yes, at the same percentage as on any other hospital policy: 24.118 % at the base income tier when everyone is under 65, 16.079 % at tier 1, 8.038 % at tier 2 and nothing at tier 3. On a cheap policy the rebate is small in dollars, but so is the premium.

lhc-overseas-returning-australians.text: Enter the days you have spent in Australia without hospital cover since your base day, leaving out your years abroad: the calculator says whether a loading applies when you rejoin. Australians who live abroad are not penalised for the years they spend away. If you are a citizen or permanent resident and were overseas on the 1 July after your 31st birthday, you avoid any Lifetime Health Cover loading by buying private hospital cover before the first anniversary of your return. Your return is your first stay in Australia of 90 days or more: shorter trips home, for a wedding or a Christmas, leave you overseas for these rules. If you already held hospital cover after your base day and cancelled it to live abroad for at least a year, the days you spend outside Australia are not taken from your lifetime allowance of 1,094 days without cover. The Ombudsman's example of Wei shows the limit: posted to Canada, he came home in 2012, waited three years to rejoin, used 1,114 days of absence and pays 2 %. Buy within the year, and nothing is added. Which of the three situations is yours? The Ombudsman's Lifetime Health Cover page treats expatriates in three groups, and the deadline is different for each. Find your row before doing any arithmetic. In every case the meaning of "return" is the same: your first period of 90 days or more in Australia. A posting abroad with a fortnight at home each summer is one continuous period overseas. Overseas on your base day: the year after you come back Phuong is an Australian citizen born on 5 April 1983. She leaves for Ecuador on 26 June 2014, a few days before the 1 July after her 31st birthday, and lives there for two years, visiting her parents five times for no more than 40 days each. She comes back for good on 25 June 2016. Her new base day is 25 June 2017. She buys hospital cover on 12 October 2018, aged 35, after that anniversary, so she pays 10 %: five years over 30. Had she bought before 25 June 2017, she would have paid nothing. On today's cheapest single policy in Queensland, $1,236 a year, her 10 % costs $124 a year for ten years. Cancelled to move abroad: the allowance waits for you Wei, born in 1971, takes out hospital cover in June 2001 with no loading and cancels it in February 2004 to work in Canada. He visits family in Australia once a year for 25 days. Those visits are well within 90 days, so none of his time abroad uses his allowance. He returns for good on 15 November 2012 with zero days of absence used, but only rejoins on 4 December 2015, 1,114 days later. That is 20 days over the 1,094, and he pays 2 %. The lesson is that the allowance is generous while you are away and runs at full speed once you are back. Every day in Australia without hospital cover after your return counts, and once the 1,094 days are spent the loading returns: your previous loading, plus 2 %, plus 2 % for each further year. The days of absence page works through the count. Abroad on 1 July 2000 When the scheme began, Australians aged 31 or over who lived overseas were treated as already covered on their base day. Haruki, a permanent resident born in 1964, moves to Sweden in May 2000 and returns for good on 7 September 2012. He has 1,094 days, to 6 September 2015, to buy cover with no loading. He waits until 14 December 2018 and pays 8 %: 2 % for each of the four years after his days of absence ended, by the Ombudsman's count. That allowance is for life; if he later lets his cover lapse while living in Australia, the gap comes off the same 1,094 days. Expats and the surcharge Coming home also restarts the Medicare levy surcharge clock if your income is over $105,000 (single, 2026-27) and you are not in a Medicare levy exemption category. The surcharge is charged for each day without hospital cover; the year you are given for Lifetime Health Cover does not suspend it. A returning single person on $150,000 pays $1,875 for a full year without cover. Visa holders and expats covers the surcharge side. Paperwork that makes the difference Your insurer cannot see your travel history. To have the correct loading applied, give it an International Movement Record from the Department of Home Affairs, which lists every departure and arrival, and, if you held cover before leaving, a clearance certificate from your former insurer. PrivateHealth.gov.au lists the cases where the movement record is needed, including people who cancelled their cover after the age of 31 and went overseas for at least 12 months. Supply the documents on or after joining, and ask the insurer to reassess. The general rule is on the Lifetime Health Cover loading page , and the parallel case of people moving to Australia for the first time on new migrants . How long do I have to buy hospital cover after moving back to Australia? If you were overseas on your base day, until the first anniversary of your return, where the return is your first period of 90 days or more in Australia. Buy after that anniversary and the loading is based on your age at the 1 July before joining. If you held cover after your base day and cancelled it to go abroad, your remaining days of absence apply instead. Do visits home while I live abroad end my time overseas? Not if each visit lasts up to 90 consecutive days. PrivateHealth.gov.au treats you as still overseas during visits of up to 90 days. A stay of 90 days or more counts as your return, and for people who had cancelled their cover, any such stay is deducted from their 1,094 days of absence. What proof of my time overseas will the insurer want? An International Movement Record, which you request from the Department of Home Affairs with its application form. It shows your exit and entry dates, so the insurer can count the days you were away. If you held cover before leaving, also ask your former insurer for a clearance certificate, which it must provide within 14 days. I was over 31 and living abroad on 1 July 2000. What applies to me? You are treated as having held hospital cover on your base day. No loading builds up while you are overseas, and once back you have 1,094 days of absence to buy cover without a loading. PrivateHealth.gov.au describes Haruki, back in 2012, who bought cover in December 2018, four years after his days ran out, and paid 8 %.

mls-170000.text: At $170,000 a single person is in tier 3. There is no rebate left, so the full premium is the price: the calculator sets it against the 1.5 % surcharge. A single income for MLS purposes of $170,000 in 2026-27 is above $164,001, the start of tier 3. Two things happen there. The surcharge reaches its highest rate, 1.5 % of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, $2,550 for a full year without hospital cover. And the private health insurance rebate drops to zero, whatever your age: the ATO only pays it when income for surcharge purposes is below the tier 3 threshold. The comparison becomes simple, because the policy costs exactly its full premium, plus any Lifetime Health Cover loading. At this income any single policy with a full premium under $212.50 a month costs less than the surcharge. In New South Wales that covers the median exempt policy, $186.10, and the median policy of the Basic, Basic Plus, Bronze, Bronze Plus, Silver tiers in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026. The full premium is the price Below tier 3, every comparison between the surcharge and a policy has to take the rebate into account, and the rebate itself changes with income and age. In tier 3 it does not exist. The ATO's eligibility page sets the condition plainly: to receive the rebate, your income for surcharge purposes must be less than the tier 3 threshold. For a single person in 2026-27 that threshold is $164,001. So at $170,000 a hospital policy costs you its full premium, plus any loading, and nothing else enters the sum. The pattern is clear from the table: at $170,000, the median exempt policy costs less than the surcharge in every state, while a median Gold policy costs more in most of them. The tax pays for mid-range cover at this income, not for the top tier. Extras lose their rebate too The rebate applies to hospital, general treatment and ambulance policies, so its end in tier 3 is felt on extras as well. An extras policy costing $1,200 a year, which got $96 of rebate in tier 2, gets nothing here. Extras do not remove the surcharge in any case: only hospital cover does. Getting back under the line You are $6,000 above the tier 2 ceiling of $164,000, where the surcharge would be $2,050 and the rebate 8.038 %. Salary sacrifice into super does not lower your tier, because reportable super contributions count in income for MLS purposes; it does lower the base the rate is charged on. Deductions you are entitled to lower taxable income, and so both. The income for MLS purposes page has the components, and the $150,000 page shows how the mix of income changes the bill in tier 2. Couples at this income For a couple, $170,000 on one side is not tier 3 unless the combined income is over $328,000. With a partner earning $60,000, the couple's $230,000 is in tier 1 of the family scale, with a rebate of 16.079 %. The family $230,000 page works through that case with children. Is there any private health insurance rebate at $170,000? No. A single person whose income for surcharge purposes is $164,001 or more is in tier 3, where the rebate is 0 % at every age, for hospital, general treatment and ambulance policies alike. If you have been taking the rebate as a premium reduction, ask your insurer to remove it, or expect to repay it when you lodge. What premium beats a tier 3 surcharge? Any policy whose full yearly premium, plus loading, is below the surcharge. At $170,000 that means under $2,550 a year, or $212.50 a month, for a single person. With no rebate in tier 3, the premium on the quote is the price, which makes the comparison easy to do yourself from any policy statement. Does cover still win at $170,000 with a late-joining loading? Often, but not always. A person who first joins at 45 carries a 30 % loading. On the median NSW single policy that gives $2,903 a year against a $2,550 surcharge. On the cheapest exempt policy, cover still wins by a wide margin.

mls-families.text: Enter both parents’ incomes and the number of dependent children: the tool applies the raised family threshold and shows each parent’s share. A family with dependent children is tested like a couple, on the parents' combined income for MLS purposes, but the threshold grows with the family. For 2026-27 it is $210,000 with one child and rises by $1,500 for each MLS dependent child after the first, so $211,500 with two, $213,000 with three and $214,500 with four. Every boundary of the tiers moves by the same amount. A child counts while under 21, or from 21 to 24 while studying full time at school, college or university; a foster child does not count. To avoid the surcharge, both parents and every dependent child need an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. A family with two children and incomes of $150,000 and $95,000 is in tier 1 and pays $2,450 for a year without cover, shared between the parents in proportion to their incomes. The family threshold by number of children The base figure is the same for a couple with no children and for a family with one child: $210,000 of combined income for MLS purposes in 2026-27. From the second child on, each MLS dependent child adds $1,500 to every boundary. The increment is modest next to the threshold, so it decides the outcome only when the family is close to a line. The table below takes parents on $130,000 and $82,500, $212,500 in all, without cover, and changes only the number of children. Who is a dependent child The ATO definition is narrower than the one insurers use for family policies. For the surcharge, a child is your dependant if they are an Australian resident, you contributed to their maintenance, and they are: under 21, or from 21 to 24 and studying full time at school, college or university. Your child includes a child born in or outside marriage, an adopted child, a newborn or newly adopted child, your spouse's child and a child within the meaning of the Family Law Act 1975, such as a child under a surrogacy order. A foster child is not included. You maintained a child if you lived in the same house, gave them food, clothing and lodging, helped pay their living, medical or education costs, or pay child support for them. A child turning 21 without full-time study counts for the part of the year before the birthday; a full-time student turning 25 counts until then. Every member must be covered Above the family threshold, a single uncovered day for any member makes the parents liable for that day. The M2 instructions give a 2025-26 example. Jill and Kevin are married with three dependent children. Jill and the children are on a hospital policy all year; Kevin is added to it on 10 January 2026. Their combined income for MLS purposes is $220,000, above their 2025-26 family threshold of $205,000 ($202,000 plus two increments of $1,500). Because not everyone was covered from 1 July 2025 to 9 January 2026, both Jill and Kevin are liable for those 193 days, Jill included, although she held cover the whole time. Each writes 172, the days without liability, at label A of question M2. The policy statement does the counting Your insurer's private health insurance statement shows, for each policy, the number of days it provided an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. Those days go into your return. If a child was added late, or one parent sat on a separate policy for part of the year, the statements show it. The ATO then works out the surcharge, if any, and adds it to the Medicare levy on your notice of assessment. Adult children and insurer rules Insurers have their own, wider notion of a dependant. Since rules passed in June 2021, a policy may cover dependants up to age 31, though each insurer can set a lower limit. That is a policy rule, not a tax one. PrivateHealth.gov.au says that a person covered as a dependant on a family hospital policy is not liable to pay the surcharge, provided they have no spouse or dependants of their own. A 26-year-old on the family policy is thus protected from the surcharge, while no longer an MLS dependant who raises the parents' threshold. What the cheapest family policy costs A family policy in the October 2026 premium file costs, for the cheapest product of every state, exactly the same as the cheapest couple policy. In Victoria the cheapest open family policy that avoids the surcharge is $204.20 a month before the rebate, the median $451.90. For the family of the summary, the comparison with a surcharge of $2,450 is on the calculator of the home page ; single parents have a page of their own. Sources Dependants and maintenance: ATO, Family and dependants for Medicare levy surcharge purposes (updated 21 August 2026) and ATO, M2 Medicare levy surcharge 2026 (tax return instructions) . Thresholds: ATO, Medicare levy surcharge income, thresholds and rates (updated 22 June 2026) . Adult dependants on family policies: PrivateHealth.gov.au, Medicare Levy Surcharge ; insurer age limits: PrivateHealth.gov.au, private health insurance changes . Does a newborn raise the family surcharge threshold? Yes, from birth. The ATO definition of a child for MLS purposes includes a child born or adopted during the income year, and a stepchild. A child counts as an MLS dependant while under 21, so the newborn adds a dependent child to the count and, from the second child on, adds to the family threshold. The baby also needs to be on a hospital policy. Is a 22-year-old at university still an MLS dependant? Yes, if they study full time. A child aged 21 to 24 who is a full-time student at school, college or university remains an MLS dependant. In the year a student turns 25, they count for the part of the year before that birthday. A child who turns 21 and is not studying full time counts only for the part of the year before turning 21. Are adult children covered on our family policy liable for the surcharge? Not as a rule. PrivateHealth.gov.au says a person covered as a dependant on a family hospital policy is not liable to pay the surcharge, as long as they have no spouse or dependants of their own. Insurer rules on the age limit for dependants vary, and an older child may need a policy of their own. Do foster children count towards the family threshold? No. The ATO page on family and dependants for MLS purposes, updated in August 2026, states that a foster child is not included as a dependant. Only your own child, an adopted child, a stepchild, a newborn or newly adopted child and a child within the meaning of the Family Law Act 1975 count. The $1,500 increments follow that list.

state-sa.text: The rebate grows with the age of the oldest person on the policy. For an Adelaide couple in their late sixties, that changes the sum. South Australia has the third lowest premiums for the cheapest hospital cover that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge, after the Northern Territory and Western Australia: $98.81 a month for one person and $197.62 for a couple before the rebate, in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026. What you pay after the rebate depends on two things, the income tier and the age of the oldest person covered. A couple on a combined $230,000 sits in family tier 1, where the rebate is 16.079 % if both are under 65, 20.098 % between 65 and 69 and 24.118 % from 70. On the cheapest couple policy that is $1,990, $1,895 or $1,799 a year, against a surcharge of $2,300 for the couple without cover. A bill before Parliament would remove the higher rates for older members from April 2027. One couple, three ages Take an Adelaide couple, one partner on $130,000 and the other on $100,000. Their combined income of $230,000 is over the family threshold of $210,000, so without hospital cover each of them pays the tier 1 rate on their own income. The table compares that with two policies: the cheapest exempt couple policy and the cheapest Silver Plus one, for three ages of the older partner. The surcharge column does not move with age: it is a tax on income, not on the policy. The net premium falls as the rebate rises. For this couple the cheapest policy costs less than the surcharge at every age. The Silver Plus policy, which covers far more, is dearer than the surcharge at 40 and still dearer at 72. A loading on either partner would add to every net figure, since the rebate is never paid on the loading. Choice in South Australia The file holds 455 open single policies and 454 couple policies that avoid the surcharge in the state, from 22 insurers. For one person, the three cheapest are close together: see-u by HBF at $98.81, ahm health insurance at $99.50 and GMHBA Limited at $102.00, all Basic tier. The median single policy, $187.46, is 1.9 times the cheapest. For couples the tiers line up like this: The excess limit on a couple policy A couple or family policy avoids the surcharge if its excess is $1,500 or less for the policy; a single policy needs $750 or less. The cheapest South Australian couple policy has an excess of $750 per person and $1,500 per policy, inside the limit. A higher excess lowers the premium but takes the policy out of the surcharge exemption, so a couple who picks a $2,000 excess to save money would pay both the premium and the surcharge. Our premium file leaves out every policy above the limits for that reason, and the excess page explains the rule. Gaps in the year count too. If the couple only takes out cover in January, each partner still owes the surcharge for the days from 1 July without it. The part-year page computes that share. Single parents A single parent is tested against the family threshold with their own income only, $210,000 with one child and $211,500 with two. Many single parents are therefore under the threshold and owe no surcharge at all. Above it, the cheapest exempt single parent policy in South Australia costs $153.00 a month before the rebate. The single parents page has the detail. Sources: PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 ( data.gov.au ), rebate rates on ato.gov.au , the bill before Parliament . Naming a policy reports a price, not a recommendation. How the figures are built . How does age change the private health insurance rebate in South Australia? The same way as everywhere: the rebate depends on the age of the oldest person on the policy. At the base tier it is 24.118 % under 65, 28.139 % from 65 to 69 and 32.158 % from 70, for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. South Australia only changes the premium the percentage is applied to. What does the cheapest couple policy cost in Adelaide? The cheapest open couple policy that avoids the surcharge in South Australia costs $197.62 a month before the rebate, from see-u by HBF, in the file of 1 October 2026. The median couple policy costs $373.21. Both prices are the published base premiums, without any age-based discount an insurer may give. Will older South Australians lose part of their rebate in 2027? Only if Parliament passes the bill introduced on 15 October 2026. It would give people aged 65 and over the under-65 rates from 1 April 2027. On a Silver Plus couple policy at $318.27 a month, a couple aged 67 in tier 1 would lose about $153 a year. It is not law.

lhc-days-of-absence.text: Add up the days you have been without hospital cover since your base day and enter your current loading: you see how many days remain, or the loading you would rejoin with. Once you have held private hospital cover on or after your Lifetime Health Cover base day, you can stop it and restart it without penalty, within a lifetime limit of 1,094 days, three years less one day. These are your days of absence. They cover the gap when you change insurer, a lean year, or a break between jobs. Some periods are not taken from them: an approved suspension of your policy, time spent overseas after you cancel cover to live abroad for at least a year, and service in the ADF. Use them up, with a total gap of 1,095 days or more, and you pay a loading when you rejoin: your previous loading, plus 2 %, plus 2 % for every further year without cover, and your ten years towards removal start again. The Ombudsman's example of Marit shows the safe side: 1,069 days without cover and her 4 % loading did not move. A budget of days, spent across your life Think of the allowance as a bank account opened on your base day with 1,094 days in it. Every day you hold hospital cover leaves it untouched; every day without cover takes one away. It is described on PrivateHealth.gov.au under the heading "permitted days without hospital cover", and it only exists if you held hospital cover on or after your base day. Someone who has never had cover has no allowance to spend: their loading simply grows with age. Marit stays inside the limit Marit was born on 12 February 1976 and took out hospital cover on 30 August 2008, aged 32, with a 4 % loading. She cancelled on 15 March 2011 and rejoined on 16 February 2014: 1,069 days without cover. That is 25 days short of the limit, so she pays the same 4 % she paid before. Had she waited another month, her gap would have passed 1,094 days, and she would have rejoined on a higher loading with a fresh ten year count. What the allowance does not pay for Several periods without an active policy are not deducted at all. The Ombudsman lists them: Approved suspensions. If your insurer agrees to suspend your hospital cover for a short period, such as an overseas holiday, those days are not taken from the 1,094. Each insurer sets its own conditions. Living overseas. If you cancel after your base day to go abroad for at least one continuous year, the days outside Australia do not count. Visits home of up to 90 consecutive days leave you overseas; longer stays are deducted. Returning from overseas has the examples. ADF service and the Gold Card. Full-time ADF members whose care comes through the ADF, and people listed on a DVA Gold Card, are treated as covered. After discharge or withdrawal of the card, the 1,094 days start. When the days run out A total gap of 1,095 days or more changes three things. First, a loading applies on rejoining: the loading you had before, plus 2 %, plus 2 % for each further year without cover. Second, the continuity of your ten loaded years is broken, and you start the count again from the date you rejoin. Third, if your loading had already been removed after ten years, you can become liable for one again. A person who had a 10 % loading and stays out 1,894 days comes back on about 16 %, which on the cheapest SA single policy costs $190 a year, for ten more years. Change insurer without spending days A switch between insurers only uses days if there is a gap between the two policies. Start the new policy the day the old one ends, and ask the old insurer for a clearance certificate: it must issue one within 14 days, and it carries your loading, your dates and the waiting periods already served. The new insurer uses it to apply the right loading. Two people, the same gap, different results The allowance only protects people who held cover on or after their base day. Take two friends who both turn 31 in 2020 and both go without hospital cover for the whole of the next four years. The first held a policy on her base day and cancelled it a month later: her gap of about four years uses up her 1,094 days and she rejoins with about 4 %, by our estimate of the Ombudsman's rule. The second never had cover: there is no allowance to spend, and on rejoining his loading is set by his age on the 1 July before he joins, 10 % at 35. The rule rewards having started, even briefly, before the deadline. Counting your own days Add every period without hospital cover since your base day, excluding approved suspensions and qualifying time overseas. Your current and former insurers can tell you their dates; the clearance certificate is the reference. If the total is close to 1,094, the safest move is to rejoin before it is reached, even with a Basic policy, then compare at leisure. Basic policies that also avoid the Medicare levy surcharge start at $98.81 a month in South Australia ( basic hospital cover ). The loading rules in full are on the Lifetime Health Cover loading page , and the ten year count on the removal page . Are the days of absence counted per gap or over my whole life? Over your whole life. The 1,094 days are a single allowance, not a number per break: two gaps of 600 days use 1,200 days and exhaust it. PrivateHealth.gov.au states the limit cannot be renewed. Keep the dates of every period without hospital cover, or ask your insurer, whose clearance certificate records them. Does suspending my policy use up days of absence? No, if your insurer agrees to the suspension. PrivateHealth.gov.au says an approved suspension, for example while you travel overseas on holiday, is not counted towards your 1,094 days. Conditions vary between insurers. A suspension does not protect you from the Medicare levy surcharge, which is still charged for the suspended days. What happens to waiting periods after a gap in cover? They may apply again. The days of absence only protect your Lifetime Health Cover loading. PrivateHealth.gov.au warns that a break in hospital cover can mean serving waiting periods again when you rejoin, for example before treatment of a pre-existing condition. Ask your insurer before you let a policy lapse. I left the ADF after my base day. How many days do I have? 1,094 days from discharge. Members on continuous full-time service whose care comes through the ADF are treated as holding hospital cover. PrivateHealth.gov.au gives the case of Megan, discharged on 14 October 2017, who bought cover on 7 March 2019 after 509 days of absence and paid no loading. Do veterans with a Gold Card have days of absence? Yes. Holding a DVA Gold Card counts as holding hospital cover. If the card is withdrawn, the holder has 1,094 days to buy a policy. The Ombudsman's example is Patrick, whose card was withdrawn on 9 June 2017 and who bought cover on 25 May 2019, after 715 days, with no loading. White and orange cards do not count.

mls-single-parents.text: Enter your income for MLS purposes and your dependent children: the tool tests you on the family threshold, as the rules do for a sole parent. A single parent with at least one MLS dependent child is not tested on the single threshold of $105,000. PrivateHealth.gov.au states that single parents, like couples, are subject to the family tiers, and the M2 instructions list the exemption for a person who was single all year with a dependent child all year: no surcharge while income for MLS purposes stays at or under $210,000 for 2026-27, plus $1,500 for each dependent child after the first. Because there is no spouse, that line is compared with the parent's own income only, which gives a sole parent twice the room of a single person without children. A parent on $170,000 with one child pays nothing, where a single person on the same income would pay $2,550 without cover. Above the family line the usual rates apply, 1 % to 1.5 %, on taxable income and fringe benefits, and every dependent child also needs hospital cover to avoid them. The same income, three situations The family line makes a large difference for a sole parent. The table compares a single person without children with a single parent of one and of three dependent children, at the same incomes for MLS purposes, without hospital cover for the whole of 2026-27. Between $105,000 and $210,000 the single person pays and the single parent does not. Above the family line the parent pays the family tier rates on their own income: on $230,000 with two children, tier 1 at 1 %, or $2,300 for the year. Which children count The child must be an Australian resident you contributed to maintaining, under 21, or 21 to 24 and in full-time study. You maintain a child if you live together, give them food, clothing and lodging, help pay their living, medical or education costs, or pay child support for them, even when they do not live with you. A foster child does not count. A stepchild does, but a single parent by definition has no current spouse whose children could be counted. The rule that surprises separated parents is the equal dependant rule. If the parents lived apart for all or part of the year and the child was a dependant of each, the ATO treats the child as an equal dependant of each parent, irrespective of the number of nights in each home. Receiving Family Tax Benefit Part A does not change that for the surcharge. Both parents may therefore use the family threshold, each on their own income. Years with a change When you become or stop being a sole parent during the year, for example when a separation happens or a youngest child turns 21 and leaves study, the M2 instructions split the year. For days with a spouse or a dependent child, you are liable only if your own income for MLS purposes is above the family threshold and someone in the family lacked cover. For days with neither spouse nor child, the single threshold of $105,000 applies. Your status on 30 June then decides whether your rate is read from the family tiers with combined income, if you had a spouse, or from the single tiers with your own income, if you were single. On the return itself, the number of dependent children you had during the year goes at question IT8, label D, and the days for which you do not have to pay the surcharge at question M2, label A. The ATO uses both to choose the threshold. An older child who is covered as a dependant on your single parent policy is not liable for the surcharge personally, as long as they have no spouse or dependants of their own. The calculator on this page assumes the same situation for the whole year. For a year with a change, run it twice, once per period, and keep the days of each. An ex-partner is not a dependant A former spouse to whom you pay maintenance or child support is not your dependant for MLS purposes. The children you support remain dependants, which is why the family threshold can still be yours after a separation even if the children live mostly with the other parent. The price of avoiding it A single parent policy covers one adult and the children, and counts as a policy for more than one person, so its excess can go up to $1,500 and still avoid the surcharge. In the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, 720 open single parent policies qualify in NSW and the ACT; the cheapest costs $156.05 a month before the rebate and the median $336.69. Western Australia is cheaper, from $119.95. Just above the line, on $211,000 with one child, the surcharge would be $2,110 against $1,572 for that cheapest NSW policy after the tier 1 rebate of 16.079 %. The home calculator sets the two side by side for your state. Sources Family tiers for single parents: PrivateHealth.gov.au . Exemption categories and changes during the year: ATO, M2 Medicare levy surcharge 2026 (tax return instructions) . Equal dependants, maintenance, child support and foster children: ATO, Family and dependants for Medicare levy surcharge purposes . Thresholds: ATO, Medicare levy surcharge income, thresholds and rates (updated 22 June 2026) . Is a single parent taxed on the single or the family MLS threshold? On the family threshold. A person who was single for the whole year and had a dependent child for the whole year is exempt while their income for MLS purposes is at or under the family threshold, $210,000 for 2026-27 with one child and $1,500 more for each further child. The parent's own income is the only one counted. Does a child who lives with the other parent count for my surcharge threshold? It can. When parents live apart, the ATO treats a child as an equal dependant of each parent, whatever the split of days in care, provided the child is a dependant of each of them. Paying child support counts as maintaining the child even if they live elsewhere. Unlike other Medicare levy rules, Family Tax Benefit Part A received by one parent does not change this. What if I became a single parent part way through the year? Then the single and family thresholds can both apply, each for its own period. The M2 instructions say that if you had a new spouse, separated, or became or ceased to be a sole parent during the year, you work out your liability separately for the days you were single, without spouse or child, and for the days you had a spouse or a dependent child. What type of policy does a single parent need to avoid the surcharge? Hospital cover for yourself and your dependent children, usually a single parent policy, with an excess of no more than $1,500 because it covers more than one person. In the October 2026 premium file the cheapest such policy in NSW and the ACT costs $156.05 a month before the rebate, against $102.60 for a single policy.

state-wa.text: Perth premiums sit well below the east coast. Enter your income to see how far the cheapest exempt policy undercuts the surcharge. A single Western Australian who earns over $105,000 of income for MLS purposes in 2026-27 and holds no hospital cover pays the Medicare levy surcharge. The cheapest open policy that removes it costs $78.86 a month before the rebate in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, about 23 % less than the cheapest one in New South Wales. The next two policies, from HBF Health Limited and ahm health insurance, are within cents of it. On $140,000 the surcharge is $1,750, while the cheapest policy costs $870 after the 8.038 % rebate, and a policy at the median price of $158.90 a month costs $1,754. The table below runs the same sum at five incomes, and the calculator above lets you set your own family, age and loading. Five incomes, one state The left column moves through the tiers: $106,000 is just inside tier 1, $125,000 in tier 2, $170,000 in tier 3 where there is no rebate. Two effects pull in opposite directions as income rises. The surcharge grows, both because the rate climbs from 1 % to 1.5 % and because it is a percentage of a larger income. The net premium grows too, because the rebate falls from 16.079 % to nothing. In Western Australia the first effect wins at every income in the table for the cheapest policy, which is why its saving column only rises. The price ladder, tier by tier The cheapest policy is a Basic one. If you want more, here is what each tier costs at its cheapest and at its median in the state, single cover, before the rebate. Two oddities stand out. Bronze Plus is cheaper at its lowest than plain Bronze, and Silver Plus cheaper than plain Silver, because the "Plus" tiers hold far more policies and some of them are priced aggressively. The tier name says what a policy must cover at least, not what it costs, so it is worth comparing across tiers rather than within one. What this means for a Perth household For most single people over the threshold, the cheapest exempt policy costs less than the surcharge in WA, as it does in every state. What is particular here is the margin. On $140,000, the cheapest policy undercuts the surcharge by $880, enough to move up to a Bronze Plus policy at $94.10 a month and still pay less than the tax. Someone who joins late with a Lifetime Health Cover loading pays more, since the loading is added after the rebate: the loading page has the figures. Couples, single parents and older members The couple and family cells follow the same pattern at double the price: $157.72 a month for the cheapest couple policy and $157.72 for a family, while a single parent pays $119.95, a little over one and a half times the single price. A Perth couple on $130,000 and $100,000 has a combined $230,000, inside family tier 1, and would pay $2,300 of surcharge between them without cover, against $1,588 for the cheapest couple policy after the rebate. For members aged 65 or more the rebate is higher, 20.098 % at tier 1 between 65 and 69, so the net premium falls further; the page for over 65s covers the bill that would change this from April 2027. All prices come from the file of 1 October 2026 on data.gov.au : 455 open single policies in WA from 22 insurers. Naming the cheapest policy is a figure, not a recommendation; check its Private Health Information Statement for what it covers. Thresholds and rebate: ATO . What is the cheapest hospital cover in WA that avoids the surcharge? In the file of 1 October 2026, a Basic policy from see-u by HBF at $78.86 a month for one person, with a $750 excess. It avoids the surcharge because the excess is within the $750 limit. We report it as the lowest price in the public data, not as advice to buy it. Is a median-priced policy in Western Australia cheaper than the surcharge? It depends on income. At $158.90 a month, a single person aged 35 without loading finds it cheaper than the surcharge from $140,500. Under that, the surcharge costs less than a mid-priced policy, though not less than the cheapest one. Do families in WA pay twice the single premium? For the cheapest policies, yes or very nearly: $157.72 a month for a family against $78.86 for one person. A single parent policy costs $119.95. The family surcharge threshold is also doubled, $210,000 of combined income, plus $1,500 per child after the first.

lhc-10-year-removal.text: Enter how long you have paid your loading and its rate: the calculator counts the months left and what the loading will still cost you before it drops. A Lifetime Health Cover loading is not for life. Once you have paid it for 10 continuous years of hospital cover, your insurer removes it and your premium falls to the standard price, for as long as you keep your cover. The ATO puts it in dollars: join at 40 and you could pay 20 % more each year for 10 years; join at 50 and it is 40 % more for 10 years. Breaks allowed under the days of absence rules do not reset the count, but they do not count towards it either, so a two year gap pushes the end date back two years. The Ombudsman's example of Kaia shows this: a 6 % loading from November 2005, nine years and two months of cover, two years abroad, then 297 more days of loading before it was removed in January 2018. If you cancel after the loading has gone, a new loading can apply when you return. Ten years, measured how? PrivateHealth.gov.au says the loading is removed once you have held it on your hospital cover for 10 continuous years. Three rules shape that count: It starts when you first pay the loading, on the day your hospital cover begins. Permitted days without hospital cover, within your 1,094 days of absence or while overseas, do not break the continuity, but they are not counted as years with cover. Using up your days of absence breaks it: the ten years start again from the day you rejoin, on a new loading. The ATO page on the loading adds the warning that applies after the end: cancel your cover once the loading is removed, and you may have to pay a loading again on a later policy.
