Kaia's count, with a break abroad Kaia, born on 7 March 1972, takes out hospital cover on 17 November 2005 with a 6 % loading, three years over 30. She cancels on 24 January 2015 to go overseas, after 3,355 days, nine years, two months and seven days of continuous cover. She does not return to Australia for more than 90 consecutive days until she comes back for good on 24 January 2017. She rejoins on 26 March 2017, pays her original 6 % for another 297 days, about ten months, and the loading is removed on 17 January 2018. Her two years abroad neither broke the count nor shortened it. What the ten years cost at each loading The total depends on the loading and on the policy carrying it. The table uses the cheapest and the median single hospital policies in Tasmania that avoid the Medicare levy surcharge, in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, with premiums rising each year by 4.41 %, the 2026 industry average. The column on the right is the reason many late joiners start low. On a median policy, a 40 % loading costs $11,245 over the ten years; on the cheapest exempt policy, $5,898. Both remove the loading on the same date. Upgrading the policy once the loading has gone costs the standard price only. Couples and the ten years On a couple or family policy the loading is the average of the adults' own loadings. PrivateHealth.gov.au shows, with the case of Archie, that a person's loading is removed after their own ten years of continuous cover, even on a shared policy. When one partner's loading is removed, the average falls: a couple with 22 % and 12 % pay 17 % on the policy, and once the first partner's loading has gone, 6 %. A partner who joins the policy later brings their own loading and their own start date. The same logic applies to a dependant with a disability who is counted as an adult on a family policy: PrivateHealth.gov.au says such a person keeps their loading when they move onto a parent's policy, and can have it removed after ten continuous years of hospital cover, like anyone else. Planning the last years Because the end date is fixed by the start of the loading plus ten years of cover, it is worth writing it down. If you joined on 1 March 2019 and never had a gap, your loading ends on 1 March 2029. A gap of 200 permitted days moves it to around mid September 2029. A gap that exhausts your days of absence wipes the count and starts a new one with a higher loading. Before cancelling in the final years, compare what you would save with what a new ten years would cost: the days of absence page gives the loading you would come back with. The Medicare levy surcharge does not wait ten years The surcharge depends only on whether you hold hospital cover in the income year and on your income. Removing the loading changes nothing there. A person on $140,000 who cancels pays $1,750 a year in surcharge in 2026-27, whatever their loading history. Is private health insurance worth it compares the two over time. The full set of rules is on the Lifetime Health Cover loading page , and the way couples share a loading is set out there as well. Do I have to stay with the same insurer for the ten years? No. The count is of continuous hospital cover, not of membership of one fund. You can change insurer or policy during the ten years. To keep the count intact, start the new policy without a gap and give the new insurer the clearance certificate from the old one, which records your loading and the dates already served. Does the loading come off on its own after ten years? Yes. The insurer applies the removal once you have held the loading on your hospital cover for ten continuous years, and the loading stays at zero while you keep your cover. If your dates are wrong, for example after several changes of insurer, ask for the dates on record and supply your clearance certificates. Is it worth taking a cheap policy just to run down the ten years? It can be. The loading is a percentage of whatever hospital premium you pay. On the cheapest exempt single policy in Tasmania, $1,205 a year before the rebate, a 20 % loading costs $241 a year; on a median policy, $459. The ten years run at the same speed on either, and a policy change does not restart them. What happens if I cancel my cover after the loading has been removed? The ATO and PrivateHealth.gov.au both warn that you may become liable for a loading again if you take out hospital cover later. Your days of absence still apply: a gap within the 1,094 day lifetime allowance leaves the loading at zero, a longer one brings a loading back with a new ten year count.

mls-part-year-cover.text: Say how many months of the income year have gone without cover: the tool compares staying uncovered to 30 June with joining today. The Medicare levy surcharge is not an all-or-nothing charge for the year. It is worked out for the number of days on which you, your spouse or a dependant lacked an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover, divided by 365. A single person on $130,000 of income for MLS purposes, which is tier 2 in 2026-27, would pay $1,625 for a full year without cover, about $4.45 a day. Take out a policy on 1 January and roughly half of that disappears. The days already gone cannot be undone, but every day after the start date of the policy is free of surcharge. Your insurer's private health insurance statement shows the number of covered days, and you report the days you are not liable at question M2 of your return. Suspending a policy, for example while travelling, does not count as cover: the surcharge runs for the suspended days. Cancelling cover to travel overseas exposes you in the same way. The formula For each person liable, the ATO applies the rate of the tier to taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, then multiplies by the share of the year without cover: surcharge = (taxable income + reportable fringe benefits) x rate x days without cover / 365 The ATO's own illustration of the fraction is Michelle, in the 2025-26 M2 instructions: $102,000 x 1 % x 262 / 365. The days counted are those on which you, your spouse or any dependent child lacked cover. If one family member joins the policy late, the whole family is charged for the uncovered days, as the families page shows with the ATO example of Jill and Kevin. Months without cover, side by side The table takes a single person in NSW on $130,000 and sets the surcharge for the months without cover against the cost, after the rebate, of the cheapest exempt policy for the rest of the year. The two columns move in opposite directions: each month of delay adds surcharge and saves premium. At this income the month of premium is cheaper than the month of surcharge, so joining sooner costs less in total. At an income just over the threshold the gap narrows, and a Lifetime Health Cover loading raises the premium side. Nothing of this shows during the year. Your employer does not withhold anything for the surcharge, so the days without cover only appear when the ATO processes your return: the amount is added to your tax liability and comes out of your refund, or adds to your bill. A policy started in May therefore saves money you would otherwise only see go when you lodge after 30 June. The ATO example: Jacinta In 2025-26, Jacinta is single with no dependants and an income for MLS purposes of $109,000, above that year's single threshold of $101,000. She takes out private patient hospital cover on 16 January 2026. From then to 30 June she is not liable: 166 days, the number she writes at label A of question M2. For the other 199 days she pays the surcharge. The ATO does not print the amount; if all of her $109,000 were taxable income, it would be about $594.27 at the tier 1 rate of 1 %. Travel, suspension and cancellation Two situations catch people out. The first is a suspension : an insurer may agree to suspend a policy and its payments during a long trip, on terms that vary from fund to fund, but PrivateHealth.gov.au is explicit that suspended days are not covered days for the surcharge. The second is cancelling to travel : the ATO warns that if you cancel your cover while overseas, you may have to pay the surcharge for that period. In both cases the ATO suggests asking your fund how much premium you would save and comparing it with the surcharge. Travel insurance and cover from an overseas fund never replace Australian hospital cover for this purpose. Suspensions help with the loading, not the surcharge A suspension your insurer approves does count in your favour for the Lifetime Health Cover loading: those days are not deducted from your 1,094 days of absence. For the surcharge, though, they are days without cover. The days of absence page explains the loading side. Status changes split the year too Days can also be counted differently because your household changed. If you married, separated, or became or stopped being a sole parent, the M2 instructions apply the single threshold to the days you were single and the family threshold to the days you had a spouse or a dependent child. The couples page works through the ATO examples of a separation in October and a wedding in January. Sources Days, label A and the Jacinta example: ATO, M2 Medicare levy surcharge 2026 (tax return instructions) . Suspension: PrivateHealth.gov.au, Medicare Levy Surcharge . Travel and overseas funds: ATO, Appropriate level of private patient hospital cover . Thresholds: ATO, Medicare levy surcharge income, thresholds and rates (updated 22 June 2026) . Premiums: data.gov.au . If I take out hospital cover in March, do I still pay the surcharge? Only for the days from 1 July until the day before your policy started, if your income for MLS purposes is above the threshold. For a single person on $130,000, eight months without cover come to about $1,082. The days from the start of the policy to 30 June carry no surcharge. Does suspending my health insurance while overseas trigger the surcharge? Yes. PrivateHealth.gov.au states that if you hold hospital cover but temporarily suspend it, for example to travel overseas, you are not exempt for the suspended period and pay the surcharge for those days. The ATO suggests asking your fund how much premium a suspension or cancellation would save and comparing it with the surcharge it would cost you. Where do I find the number of days I was covered? On the private health insurance statement your insurer sends after 30 June. It gives, for each policy, the number of days the policy provided an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. You use it to fill question M2, where label A takes the number of days for which you do not have to pay the surcharge. Does travel insurance count as cover for the days I am away? No. The ATO states that travel insurance is not private patient hospital cover for the surcharge, and that cover provided by an overseas fund does not count either. Only a policy for hospital treatment in Australia from a registered Australian health insurer stops the days from being charged, with an excess within the limits.

state-tas.text: In Tasmania the lowest list price and the lowest price you can pay are not always the same policy. Your age decides. The cheapest open hospital policy that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge in Tasmania is Basic Hospital Accident Only $750/$1500 Excess from HBF Health Limited, at $100.42 a month for one person before the rebate in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026. Unlike the cheapest policies of most other states, it offers no age-based discount. The next one, from see-u by HBF at $103.39, does: insurers may take up to 10 % off the hospital premium of someone who joined between 18 and 25, which would bring it to $93.05. The surcharge does not care about age: a 28-year-old on $115,000 without cover pays $1,150, exactly what a 50-year-old on the same income pays. The calculator above uses list prices; this page shows where a discount changes the ranking, and the price of every hospital tier in the state. List price against what a young member pays The table applies the largest allowed discount by joining age to the three cheapest single policies of the state. It is the maximum an insurer may offer, not a promise: check the policy, since a discount is attached to the product. For someone who joins at 25 or younger, the second policy on list price becomes the cheapest by a few dollars a month. At 29 the discount is only 2 % and the ranking barely moves. The rebate is then worked out on the premium you actually pay. Our calculator sticks to list prices, the figure the file publishes; if you hold a discount, type your own premium in the folded options. Why young high earners face the question early The surcharge threshold applies from the first dollar over $105,000, whatever your age. A Tasmanian in their late twenties on $115,000 is in tier 1 and would pay $1,150 without cover. The cheapest exempt policy costs $1,011 after the 16.079 % rebate. Holding hospital cover before the 1 July after your 31st birthday also avoids the Lifetime Health Cover loading for life, as long as you keep it: the base day page explains the date. Couples, dependants and the age of 41 On a couple or family policy the discount is averaged between the two adults, as the Lifetime Health Cover loading is: one partner with 10 % and the other with 6 % give 8 % on the policy, the Ombudsman's own example. A young adult covered as a dependant on a parent's family policy gets no discount; they can have their own policy with a discount or be a dependant, not both. Once granted, the discount stays until the member turns 41, then shrinks by 2 % a year until it reaches zero. If you switch policy or insurer, ask first whether your discount moves with you: insurers decide whether to honour it on transfer. For a Tasmanian couple the cheapest exempt policy on list price is $200.84 a month, and for a family $200.84; a single parent pays $157.45. A couple on a combined $250,000, $160,000 and $90,000, would pay $3,125 of surcharge between them without cover, against $2,216 a year for that couple policy after the rebate. Every tier at its cheapest in Tasmania The pattern of the other states holds here: the "Plus" tiers have many more policies than the plain ones, and their cheapest entries can undercut the plain tier below them. The state has 446 open single policies from 22 insurers in the file, about the same choice as the mainland. Prices: PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026 ( data.gov.au ). Discounts: PrivateHealth.gov.au (Ombudsman), Age-based discount . Thresholds and rebate: ATO . Naming a policy here reports a price, it is not a recommendation. How the figures are built . What is the age-based discount on hospital cover? Insurers may offer people aged 18 to 29 a discount of 2 % for each year under 30 at the time they join, up to 10 % for ages 18 to 25. It is kept until 41, then falls by 2 % a year. It is optional for the insurer, which is why some policies have it and some do not. Does the cheapest Tasmanian policy cover more than accidents? Its name in the file is "Basic Hospital Accident Only $750/$1500 Excess", which describes what it is built for. It is a Basic tier policy with a $750 excess, enough to avoid the surcharge. What it pays for is listed in its Private Health Information Statement; read it before relying on the policy for planned treatment. How much does Gold hospital cover cost in Tasmania? The cheapest Gold policy for one person costs $246.40 a month before the rebate, from St Lukes, and the median Gold policy $372.50. For a family, the cheapest Gold policy is $492.80. At those prices Gold costs more than the surcharge for most single people under tier 3.

mls-hospital-cover-excess.text: Pick who the policy covers and type its yearly excess: the answer says at once whether the policy is an appropriate level of cover for the surcharge. A hospital policy only protects you from the Medicare levy surcharge if its excess stays within a limit: $750 or less on a policy that covers one person, $1,500 or less on every other policy, couples and families included. The ATO calls a policy within those limits an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. The excess is the amount you pay before your insurer pays for a claim, and PrivateHealth.gov.au adds that the limit is a yearly total: if you are admitted several times in the same year, the excess you pay across those stays cannot go beyond $750 or $1,500. The tier of the policy does not matter, nor the price, nor whether it comes with extras. A single person with an income for MLS purposes of $140,000 who holds a policy with a higher excess is treated as having no cover and owes $1,750 of surcharge for 2026-27. The calculator above tells you which side of the line your policy sits on. Two numbers, and what they apply to The rule is short. The ATO defines an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover as cover that a registered health insurer provides for hospital treatment in Australia, with an excess of $750 or less on a policy covering only one person, or $1,500 or less on all other policies. Everything else in this page follows from those two sentences. Notice what the limit is attached to: the number of people on the policy, not your marital status. A person in a couple who holds a policy in their own name only is on a single policy, so the lower $750 limit applies to it. And the surcharge test then asks whether your spouse and your dependants were covered too. The family side of that question is on the couples page . What the excess is, and what it is not The excess is the amount you agree to pay yourself before the insurer pays for a hospital claim. Raising it lowers the premium, which is why policies with an excess at the top of the allowed range are among the cheapest that do the tax job. In the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026, the cheapest single policy that avoids the surcharge in New South Wales and the ACT, ahm health insurance's ambulance hospital (basic), carries an excess of $750, exactly the limit. The cheapest couple policy in the same state has a per-person excess of $750 and a policy maximum of $1,500. The limit is about the excess alone. It says nothing about which treatments the policy covers. A Basic policy that covers very little passes the test as well as a Gold one, provided the excess is low enough. It also says nothing about extras: a dental or optical policy with no excess at all does not avoid the surcharge, because extras cover is not hospital cover. Travel insurance and cover from an overseas fund are not hospital cover for the surcharge either. Why a few hundred dollars of excess can cost you the surcharge Insurers sell policies with excesses above the limits, and they can make sense for someone below the income threshold who wants cheap cover for a large hospital bill. For anyone above the threshold, the arithmetic changes. Take a single person with an income for MLS purposes of $140,000. On a policy with an excess within $750, there is no surcharge. Move to a policy with a higher excess and the ATO treats the year as uncovered: the surcharge is 1.25 % of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, $1,750 for the full year in 2026-27. The premium you saved by choosing the higher excess has to beat that figure, which it rarely does at the bottom of the market. The same reasoning applies in reverse when you compare quotes. Two policies a few dollars apart may sit on different sides of the line. Check the excess first, then the price. The basic hospital cover page lists the cheapest policies within the limits in each state. The yearly cap PrivateHealth.gov.au spells out a detail the ATO page leaves implicit: the limits are yearly totals. If you are admitted to hospital twice in a year, the excess you pay across both stays cannot exceed $750 on a single policy or $1,500 on a couple or family policy. Policies built that way show an excess per admission and a maximum per year in their Private Health Information Statement. It is the yearly maximum that you compare with the limit. A protection from 2000 for long-standing members A small group of members keep an older right. PrivateHealth.gov.au states that a high-income earner who bought a hospital policy with an excess above the limits of the time on or before 24 May 2000 stays exempt from the surcharge while keeping continuous membership of that same hospital policy. Moving to another product ends it. How the limits have moved The current limits have applied since 1 April 2019, as part of the reforms that also created the Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic tiers. Before that date the maximum excess that avoided the surcharge was lower. A policy that was within the old limits is within the new ones; the change only opened the door to policies with a larger excess. Checking your own policy Three documents tell you where you stand. The Private Health Information Statement of the policy gives its excess and its tier. A statement from your insurer, which the ATO says you can ask for, gives the number of days you and your dependants held an appropriate level of cover, which is the figure your tax return needs. And if you are unsure, the ATO's advice is to ask your registered health insurer, which knows how its own excess works. Our calculator only checks the number you type against the two limits; it cannot read the conditions of a policy. If your policy falls outside the limits for part of the year, for instance because you changed product in March, the surcharge counts the days without appropriate cover. Part-year cover works that out, and the method page explains how the premiums in our tables are filtered on these same limits. What is the maximum excess to avoid the Medicare levy surcharge? $750 a year on a hospital policy that covers only one person and $1,500 a year on any other policy, such as a couple, single parent or family policy. Those limits come from the ATO's definition of an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover. A policy with a higher excess still pays hospital benefits, but for the surcharge it counts as no cover at all. Does the excess limit apply per claim or per year? Per year. PrivateHealth.gov.au explains that when several hospital claims are made in the same year, the excess you pay in total cannot exceed $750 for a single or $1,500 for a couple or family. A policy that charges its excess on every admission without a yearly cap above those amounts would not meet the rule. Is a co-payment the same as an excess for the surcharge? The ATO and PrivateHealth.gov.au set the limit on the excess, the amount you pay before your insurer pays for a claim. Some policies also charge a daily co-payment during a stay. The rules we read do not fold co-payments into the limit, so ask your insurer, who is the one that confirms whether a policy is an appropriate level of cover for the surcharge. My policy had a high excess before 2000. Do I pay the surcharge? Possibly not. PrivateHealth.gov.au says a person who bought a hospital policy with a higher excess than the limits of the time, on or before 24 May 2000, stays exempt from the surcharge while keeping continuous membership of that same hospital policy. Changing to another product ends that protection, and the current limits then apply. Who confirms whether my policy meets the excess limits? Your registered health insurer. The ATO tells taxpayers who are unsure whether their cover is at the appropriate level to ask their insurer, and you can ask the insurer for a statement of the days you and your dependants held an appropriate level of cover. Your Private Health Information Statement for the policy also shows its excess, which you can type into the calculator above.

state-nt.text: Territory premiums are a fraction of those in the southern states, so the sum between surcharge and cover gives a very clear answer here. In the Northern Territory the cheapest open hospital policy that avoids the Medicare levy surcharge costs $39.30 a month for a single person before the rebate, $472 a year, in the PrivateHealth.gov.au file of 1 October 2026. That is about 2.6 times less than the cheapest equivalent in New South Wales. The surcharge, on the other hand, is a federal tax and costs the same in Darwin as in Sydney: $1,100 on an income of $110,000, $1,750 on $140,000. After the rebate the cheapest Territory policy costs $396 a year at the first income and $434 at the second. Even the cheapest Gold policy, at $129.90 a month, beats the surcharge from $123,500. The calculator above starts on the Territory; change the income, the family or the age. Every hospital tier beats the surcharge somewhere In most states the question is whether a Basic policy is cheaper than the surcharge. In the Territory the question shifts: from which income is a better policy also cheaper than the tax? The table gives, for each hospital tier, the cheapest open policy in the October 2026 file and the lowest single income at which its net cost, after the rebate, falls under the surcharge. The result is unusual. A single Territorian on $130,000 who wants more than an accident policy can buy a Silver Plus policy for $69.45 a month, and it still costs less after the rebate than the $1,625 surcharge. Even the median exempt policy at $108.15 wins from $109,000. In New South Wales the median exempt single policy costs $186.10 a month, and at that price it only beats the surcharge from $164,500. In relative terms the ladder is steeper here: the cheapest Gold policy costs 3.3 times the cheapest Basic one, against 2.4 times in NSW, but the dollars at stake are small. Families and couples For a couple, the cheapest exempt policy is $78.60 a month, and for a family $78.60, twice the single price as is usual. A single parent pays $64.00. A Territory couple on a combined $240,000, split $150,000 and $90,000, would pay $2,400 of surcharge between them without cover; the cheapest couple policy costs $792 after the rebate. The couples page explains how the combined test and the separate bills work. Read the policy before you buy it The cheapest Territory policy, from ahm health insurance, is a Basic policy with a $750 excess. Basic is the lowest of the four hospital tiers, and the cheapest Basic policies tend to cover little beyond what the tier requires. That is enough to avoid the surcharge, because the tax rule looks at the excess and not the tier, but it may not be enough if you want to be treated as a private patient for planned surgery. Each policy's Private Health Information Statement lists what it covers. Naming the cheapest policy in the public file is a figure for the comparison, not a recommendation. Because premiums are so low, the Lifetime Health Cover loading costs less in dollars here too. A 30 % loading on the cheapest single policy adds $141 a year, against $369 in NSW. The rule itself is national: see Lifetime Health Cover loading . Where the numbers come from The prices are those of the PrivateHealth.gov.au product file of 1 October 2026 ( data.gov.au ): 448 open policies that avoid the surcharge for a single person in the Territory, from 21 insurers. The rebate and thresholds come from the ATO . Premiums change on 1 April each year. The method page lists the filters. Why are hospital premiums so low in the Northern Territory? The public file gives prices, not reasons, so we do not guess. What it shows is consistent across insurers: the cheapest single policy is $39.30 a month, the next two are $40.00 and $40.95, and the median exempt policy is $108.15. Insurers set Territory premiums separately from those of other states. How many policies avoid the surcharge in the Northern Territory? For a single person, 448 open policies from 21 insurers in the file of 1 October 2026, counting each excess option separately. For a family the count is 847. Every hospital tier is on offer, from Basic at $39.30 a month to Gold at $129.90, all before the rebate. Is the surcharge lower in the Territory? No. The Medicare levy surcharge is a federal tax with the same thresholds and rates everywhere: no surcharge up to $105,000 for a single person in 2026-27, then 1 % to 1.5 %. Only the price of the cover that avoids it changes from one state to another.

mls-fringe-benefits-salary-packaging.text: Type your taxable income and the reportable fringe benefits amount from your income statement: the tier and the surcharge without cover follow. Salary packaging lowers your taxable income, but it does not lower the income the ATO uses for the Medicare levy surcharge. Your reportable fringe benefits, the grossed-up amount shown on your income statement, are added back in full when the ATO works out your income for MLS purposes, so they can lift you over the $105,000 single threshold for 2026-27 or into a higher tier. They then count a second time: the surcharge rate is charged on taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits, not on taxable income alone. The ATO's own example for 2026-27 is Tom, a single 35-year-old with $90,000 of taxable income and $27,000 of reportable fringe benefits. His taxable income alone would be under the threshold, yet his income for MLS purposes is $117,000, tier 1, and he owes $1,170 without hospital cover. The calculator above repeats that sum with your figures. Why packaged income comes back for the surcharge Income tax and the Medicare levy surcharge do not look at the same number. Income tax starts from taxable income, which a salary packaging arrangement reduces. The surcharge starts from a wider figure, income for MLS purposes, which the ATO builds by adding several amounts back to taxable income. Reportable fringe benefits are one of them. The others are reportable super contributions, net investment losses and amounts on which family trust distribution tax has been paid, and the income for MLS purposes page goes through each line of the worksheet. The reason a fringe benefit matters more than the other add-backs is the second step. Once the tier is known, the ATO applies its rate to taxable income, total reportable fringe benefits and any amount taxed as a family trust distribution. Super contributions and investment losses are left out of that base. Fringe benefits are not. A packaged benefit is therefore treated, for the surcharge, almost exactly like salary. How fringe benefits move the tier The table holds taxable income at $95,000 for a single person without hospital cover and raises the reportable fringe benefits amount. Every figure comes from the 2026-27 thresholds read on ato.gov.au . With no packaged benefits, this person is $10,000 under the threshold and owes $0. A packaging arrangement that reports $20,000 of benefits takes the same person to $1,150 of surcharge if they hold no hospital cover. The surcharge is then charged on the whole of the taxable income plus the benefits, not only on the part above the threshold. The grossed-up figure, not the cash value The amount that counts is the reportable fringe benefits amount your employer reports, the grossed-up figure, not what the benefit would cost you in cash. The M2 instructions of the tax return take it from question IT1, labels N and W, where the reportable amounts from your income statements are recorded. If you had two employers that packaged benefits during the year, add both. When the employer also pays the premium Some packages include private health insurance itself. The ATO is clear that whoever pays the premium, each adult on the policy is income tested for the rebate, and an employee whose employer pays the premium generally receives the rebate as a reduced premium. The test uses the same income for surcharge purposes, fringe benefits included, so a packaged policy can lower your rebate percentage. In 2026-27, a single person under 65 with $95,000 of income for surcharge purposes receives 24.118 %; at $115,000 the rebate falls to 16.079 %. The Belinda example The ATO describes Belinda, single, whose employer pays her hospital cover under a salary sacrifice arrangement. Her employer paid reduced premiums based on her tier 2 income. A promotion during the year took her income for surcharge purposes into tier 3, where no rebate is paid, and she did not tell her insurer. At tax time she had a liability for the excess private health insurance reduction she had received. If your package changes, tell the insurer, or set aside the difference. Couples on packaged salaries For a couple or a family, the tier comes from the combined income for MLS purposes of both partners, and each one adds their own fringe benefits to it. Each partner then pays the rate of the household tier on their own taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, for the days they lacked cover. A packaged salary on one side can therefore move both partners into the surcharge even when the other partner's income is modest. The couples page has the full calculation. What packaging cannot do Salary packaging does not create an exemption from the surcharge, and no amount of restructuring a package changes the test: an income over the threshold without an appropriate level of hospital cover leads to the surcharge for the days concerned. The only ways out are a policy that avoids it, an exemption category, or an income for MLS purposes at or under the threshold. The cover or surcharge comparison shows which of the first two costs less for you. Do reportable fringe benefits count for the Medicare levy surcharge? Yes, twice. They are part of your income for MLS purposes, which decides whether you pass the threshold and which tier applies, and the surcharge rate is then charged on your taxable income plus your total reportable fringe benefits. A packaged benefit therefore raises both the tier and the amount the rate is applied to. Where do I find my reportable fringe benefits amount? On the income statement or payment summary from your employer. On the tax return it goes in the income tests section, and the M2 worksheet takes the total from question IT1, labels N and W. If you have more than one employer with packaged benefits, the amounts are added. Use the grossed-up figure your employer reports, not the cash value of the benefit. Can salary packaging push me into the surcharge? It can. Take $95,000 of taxable income and no packaged benefits: that is under the $105,000 threshold, so no surcharge. Add $20,000 of reportable fringe benefits and your income for MLS purposes becomes $115,000, which is tier 1, and the surcharge without hospital cover is $1,150 for 2026-27. My employer pays my health insurance. Who gets the rebate? You do, through a reduced premium, and it is your own income for surcharge purposes that decides the rebate percentage. The ATO gives the case of Belinda, whose employer pays her premiums under a salary sacrifice arrangement: when a promotion moved her into tier 3 and nobody told the insurer, she had a tax liability at the end of the year for the excess rebate received. Does a partner on a packaged salary change our family tier? Yes. For a couple, the tier comes from combined income for MLS purposes, and each partner's reportable fringe benefits are part of their own figure. Each partner then pays the rate on their own taxable income and fringe benefits. A partner with packaged benefits can therefore move the whole household above the $210,000 family threshold.

mls-investment-losses-super.text: Enter your taxable income, then your net investment losses and reportable super contributions: you see the tier they put you in and the surcharge that follows. Negative gearing and extra super contributions both lower your taxable income, and the ATO undoes both for the Medicare levy surcharge test. Your net rental property loss, your net financial investment loss, your reportable employer super contributions and your deductible personal super contributions are all added back to taxable income to give your income for MLS purposes, the figure compared with the $105,000 single threshold for 2026-27. They stop there. The surcharge rate itself is charged only on taxable income, reportable fringe benefits and any amount taxed as a family trust distribution. The ATO example of Josh shows both halves: $90,000 of taxable income, $20,000 of fringe benefits and $17,000 of net investment losses give $127,000, tier 2, but the 1.25 % rate falls on $110,000 only, $1,375. Add-backs can raise your tier, and therefore your rate, without ever being taxed themselves. Two tests, one tax The surcharge is easiest to understand as two separate questions asked of two different incomes. The first question is which tier you are in, and it uses income for MLS purposes , which starts from taxable income and adds back reportable fringe benefits, reportable super contributions, net investment losses and amounts taxed as family trust distributions. The second question is how much you pay, and it uses a narrower base: taxable income, reportable fringe benefits and family trust distribution amounts. Investment losses and super contributions appear in the first list and not in the second. That gap is the whole subject of this page. Negative gearing: the loss comes back for the tier Take a single person earning a salary of $140,000 who owns a rental property with a net loss of $25,000. Their taxable income is $115,000, and on that figure alone they would be in tier 1, paying $1,150 without cover. The ATO adds the loss back: income for MLS purposes is $140,000, which is tier 2. The rate of that tier, 1.25 %, is then charged on the taxable income of $115,000, not on $140,000. The surcharge without hospital cover is $1,438, $288 more than the taxable income alone would suggest, entirely because of the higher tier. Super contributions: same logic, smaller amounts A deductible personal super contribution lowers taxable income in the same way. A person on $112,000 who claims a deduction for a $12,000 personal contribution has a taxable income of $100,000, under the threshold. The ATO adds the contribution back, so income for MLS purposes stays at $112,000, tier 1. The 1.00 % rate is then charged on the taxable income of $100,000, $1,000 without cover, against $1,120 if the same $112,000 had all been taxable income. The contribution has not removed the surcharge, but it has lowered the amount it is charged on. Reportable employer super contributions, the amount your income statement reports under that name, are treated the same way. The M2 worksheet takes them from question IT2, label T, and deductible personal contributions from question D12, label H, of the supplementary return. Where the losses push you over a line The effect is sharpest just below a threshold. The table keeps taxable income at $100,000 for a single person and raises the add-backs, losses or super, from nothing. The charged amount never moves: it is always the same $100,000. Only the rate climbs, from nothing to 1 % and then 1.25 %, as the add-backs grow. For an investor whose losses vary from year to year, the tier can change even when salary does not. Couples: each partner's add-backs join the family total For a couple or family, the tier comes from the combined income for MLS purposes of both partners, so one partner's rental loss raises the household's figure against the $210,000 family threshold. Each partner then pays the rate on their own taxable income and fringe benefits. A spouse with a large negatively geared property and a small salary can therefore move the other partner into the surcharge. The couples page shows the split. The same income test sets your rebate The private health insurance rebate uses the same income for surcharge purposes, with the same add-backs. A rental loss that moves you from the base tier to tier 1 also lowers your rebate, from 24.118 % to 16.079 % under 65. See the rebate page . What the add-backs do not include Only the items on the ATO list are added back, and one amount is expressly taken out: an assessable first home super saver released amount does not count in the taxable income used for the test. If you had exempt foreign employment income and a taxable income of at least one dollar, the ATO asks you to add that income to taxable income on the worksheet. The income for MLS purposes page has the full worksheet, and the method page explains which items our calculator models. Are rental property losses added back for the Medicare levy surcharge? Yes. Your net rental property loss, the amount by which rental deductions exceeded rental income, is added to taxable income to work out income for MLS purposes. It can push you over the $105,000 threshold or into a higher tier. The surcharge rate is then charged on taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, so the loss itself is not charged. Do super contributions count towards the surcharge threshold? Reportable super contributions do: the total of your reportable employer super contributions and your deductible personal super contributions. Both are added to taxable income when the ATO works out income for MLS purposes. They are not part of the amount the surcharge rate is charged on, so they change your tier but are never charged at the rate. Do share trading losses count the same way as rental losses? A net financial investment loss, where your financial investment deductions exceed your financial investment income, is added back in the same way as a rental loss. The ATO adds the two together as total net investment losses. On the tax return the M2 worksheet takes them from questions IT5 and IT6 of the income tests section. Is a first home super saver release counted in income for MLS purposes? No. The ATO excludes any assessable first home super saver released amount from the taxable income used to work out income for MLS purposes. A release under that scheme therefore does not raise your surcharge tier, even though it is assessable income for income tax in the year you receive it.

mls-visa-holders-expats.text: Enter the days of 2026-27 for which you hold a Medicare levy exemption and your income: the surcharge is charged on the other days only. Temporary residents who are not entitled to Medicare and foreign residents for tax purposes usually pay no Medicare levy surcharge, but not because of their visa. They pay none because they qualify for a Medicare levy exemption, and the ATO's rule is that a person in a Medicare levy exemption category for a period is also exempt from the surcharge for that period. The condition that catches people is the family one: the exemption only works if you have no dependants for the period, or if all your dependants, your spouse included, are in an exemption category too. A temporary resident shows the period with a Medicare Entitlement Statement from Services Australia. Overseas Visitors Health Cover and Overseas Student Health Cover do not count as hospital cover for the surcharge, and neither does a policy from an overseas insurer. For a single person with $135,000 of income for MLS purposes and no exemption, the 2026-27 surcharge is $1,688 for the full year; the calculator above removes your exempt days. The exemption comes from the levy, not from the visa There is no surcharge rule written for visa holders or for Australians abroad. There are two general rules that meet. The first is in the M2 instructions of the tax return: you are exempt from the surcharge for any period in which you and all your dependants either held an appropriate level of private patient hospital cover or were in a Medicare levy exemption category. The second is the list of those categories, on the ATO's Medicare levy exemption pages. Two of them matter here. Not entitled to Medicare benefits. A temporary resident for Medicare purposes who has a Medicare Entitlement Statement for a period can claim a full levy exemption for it, known as category 3 on the return. Foreign resident for tax purposes. A foreign resident for the full year can claim a full levy exemption, known as category 2; for part of a year, the exemption covers that period. Both carry the same proviso: you had no dependants during the period, or all your dependants, including your spouse, were in a Medicare levy exemption category for it. The ATO's guidance for overseas visitors states the consequence in a line: if you qualify for a Medicare levy exemption, you are also exempt from paying the Medicare levy surcharge. Priya and Jed: the spouse decides The ATO gives two examples for 2025-26. Priya held a Temporary Skill Shortage visa, subclass 482, had no dependants and was not entitled to Medicare benefits. With a Medicare Entitlement Statement for the full year she claims a full exemption for all 365 days. Jed held the same visa and was not entitled to Medicare either, but his spouse was. Because his spouse was not in an exemption category, Jed cannot claim the exemption, despite his statement. For the surcharge, that means Jed's days are tested like a resident's: if his income for MLS purposes, combined with his spouse's, is above the family threshold and they hold no appropriate hospital cover, the surcharge applies. Before you lodge Applications for a Medicare Entitlement Statement open on 1 July and are made online through myGov. The ATO warns that processing can take up to eight weeks and that you must wait for the statement before lodging your return. Keep a copy: it is the evidence for the exempt period. What does not count as cover Many temporary residents hold health insurance because their visa requires it, and assume it settles the surcharge question. It does not. PrivateHealth.gov.au lists the policies that do not provide an exemption from the surcharge: general treatment cover without hospital cover, Overseas Visitors Health Cover, Overseas Student Health Cover, and cover held with non-registered insurers such as international ones. The ATO adds that travel insurance is not private patient hospital cover, and that cover from an overseas fund is not either. Visitors with OVHC or OSHC answer No at label E of question M2 and record at label A the number of days they are exempt. A visitor who is not eligible for Medicare may still buy a complying policy from an Australian insurer. It earns no rebate, and the ATO asks such visitors to delete any pre-filled private health insurance details before they lodge in myTax, answer No to the cover question, and give the number of days they do not have to pay the surcharge, usually 365. Exempt for part of the year Arrivals, departures and changes of visa rarely fall on 1 July. The surcharge is charged per day, so only the days outside the exemption, without appropriate hospital cover, are charged. For a single person with $135,000 of income for MLS purposes in 2026-27, the table shows the surcharge by number of exempt days. Reciprocal agreements: a policy that does the tax job only Visitors from a country with a reciprocal health care agreement have reciprocal Medicare benefits, and PrivateHealth.gov.au answers their question directly: such a visitor who earns over the threshold can avoid the surcharge by buying an approved hospital policy. It adds a frank warning: for people with reciprocal benefits, that policy will provide limited benefits for hospital treatment, and large costs follow an admission as a private patient. The comparison on is private health insurance worth it tells you whether the premium or the surcharge costs less. Australians abroad and coming home An Australian who becomes a foreign resident for tax purposes while working overseas can claim the levy exemption for that period, on the same family condition. On return, the residency days are tested normally, and the Lifetime Health Cover rules give returning Australians extra time before a loading applies: returning from overseas has the dates. Cancelling an Australian hospital policy before leaving can bring the surcharge for the days you remain a resident without cover, which the ATO suggests weighing against the premium you save. Do temporary visa holders pay the Medicare levy surcharge? Not for the days they are in a Medicare levy exemption category. A temporary resident who was not entitled to Medicare benefits can claim a full levy exemption with a Medicare Entitlement Statement, and that exemption also covers the surcharge, provided they had no dependants or every dependant, the spouse included, was exempt as well. Holding a visa alone does not exempt anyone. Does Overseas Visitors Health Cover avoid the surcharge? No. PrivateHealth.gov.au lists Overseas Visitors Cover and Overseas Student Health Cover among the policies that do not provide an exemption, and the ATO says they are not complying policies and earn no rebate. A visitor with OVHC who is not otherwise exempt answers No at label E of question M2 and records the days for which they are exempt. How long does a Medicare Entitlement Statement take? Up to eight weeks, according to the ATO. Applications open on 1 July and are made online through myGov. The ATO asks you to wait until you receive the statement before you lodge your tax return, so apply as soon as the income year ends. The statement shows the period in the year for which you were not entitled to Medicare benefits. I am covered by a reciprocal health care agreement. Can I avoid the surcharge? PrivateHealth.gov.au says yes, by buying an approved hospital policy from a registered Australian insurer. It warns that for people with reciprocal Medicare benefits such a policy provides limited benefits for hospital treatment, and that you would face significant costs as a private patient. You may prefer to compare the surcharge with the premium before buying. Does an expat who is a foreign resident for tax pay the surcharge? A foreign resident for tax purposes for the full year can claim a full exemption from the Medicare levy, which also removes the surcharge. For part of a year, the levy exemption applies to that period if you had no dependants or all your dependants were in an exemption category. The days you were an Australian resident are tested in the usual way.

medicare-levy-vs-surcharge.text: Type your taxable income and say whether you held hospital cover: the levy, the surcharge and the total appear on separate lines. The Medicare levy and the Medicare levy surcharge share a name and a line on your notice of assessment, but they are two different charges. The Medicare levy is 2 %, paid by most Australian taxpayers whether or not they hold private health insurance; people on low incomes have it reduced or removed, and some groups, such as foreign residents and temporary residents not entitled to Medicare, can claim an exemption. The surcharge is an extra 1 % to 1.5 %, paid only by people whose income for MLS purposes is above the threshold, $105,000 for a single person in 2026-27, and who do not hold an appropriate level of private hospital cover. Private hospital cover removes the surcharge, never the levy. At $130,000 of taxable income without cover, a single person pays $2,600 of levy and $1,625 of surcharge. The ATO adds the two and shows them as one amount. Side by side The surcharge has a purpose of its own: PrivateHealth.gov.au describes it as a way to encourage people on higher incomes to take out private hospital cover and, where possible, to use the private system, which reduces demand on the public one. That is why the surcharge, and only the surcharge, disappears when you hold an appropriate hospital policy. What the two cost together For a single person without dependants and without hospital cover, the table adds the levy to the 2026-27 surcharge. The levy is shown at the full rate; it is lower only for incomes far below the first row. Below the threshold, the total share is the levy alone. The first dollar over the threshold switches the surcharge on for the whole income, not for the part above it, so the total share jumps from 2 % to 3 % in a single step. It climbs again at each tier boundary, to 3.5 % at the top, where a person without cover pays three quarters of the levy again on top of it. The low-income reduction belongs to the levy only People on low incomes do not pay the full levy. For 2025-26, the latest year the ATO has published, a single taxpayer whose taxable income is $28,011 or less pays no levy at all, and between $28,011 and $35,013 the levy is reduced; the ATO works out the reduction when it assesses the return. For people entitled to the seniors and pensioners tax offset, the lines are $44,268 and $55,335. A family can also qualify for a reduction based on family taxable income. None of this touches the surcharge, which never applies at such incomes anyway. The 2026-27 low-income lines are upcoming: they were not published on 19 October 2026, and we will enter them on the day they are. Exemptions: one door, two charges A Medicare levy exemption works for both charges. The ATO lists exemptions for certain medical conditions, for foreign residents and for people who were not entitled to Medicare benefits, and the M2 instructions treat anyone in a levy exemption category for a period as exempt from the surcharge for that period, as long as all their dependants were also covered or exempt. A temporary resident with a Medicare Entitlement Statement and no dependants therefore pays neither the levy nor the surcharge for the days on the statement. Visa holders and expats sets out who qualifies. The surcharge is not withheld Your employer withholds tax with the levy in mind, but the ATO says plainly that the surcharge is not covered by the tax your employer withholds. It is added when your return is assessed. For a person who crosses the threshold for the first time without cover, it may mean a smaller refund or a tax bill. The thresholds page tells you whether that applies to you this year. Couples: one test is personal, the other is shared Each partner's Medicare levy is worked out on their own return, from their own taxable income. The surcharge is different: the tier comes from the couple's combined income for MLS purposes, tested against the family threshold of $210,000, and each partner then pays the rate of that tier on their own taxable income and reportable fringe benefits. Two partners on $120,000 each pay the full levy on their own income, and if they hold no hospital cover they also share a family tier set by $240,000 of combined income. Cover for one partner only is not enough: the ATO requires an appropriate level of cover for you, your spouse and all your dependants. The couples page works through the split. Reading your notice of assessment The ATO works out both amounts from what your return says and prints them together, as Medicare levy and surcharge. If the line looks higher than 2 % of your taxable income, the difference is usually the surcharge, or a part-year of it. Rebuild it from the M2 question: the number of days you and your dependants held an appropriate level of hospital cover, your income for MLS purposes, and your tier. The income for MLS purposes page explains the income, and part-year cover the days. Does private health insurance stop me paying the Medicare levy? No. Hospital cover only removes the surcharge. The 2 % Medicare levy is paid by most taxpayers whatever insurance they hold. It is reduced for people on low incomes and can be removed through an exemption, for instance for foreign residents or for temporary residents who are not entitled to Medicare and hold a Medicare Entitlement Statement. Is the Medicare levy surcharge taken out of my pay? Not automatically. The ATO says the surcharge is not covered by the tax your employer withholds. It is worked out when your return is processed and added to your tax liability, which can reduce a refund or create a bill. Knowing the figure early lets you set the money aside or compare it with a policy. Why does my notice of assessment show one Medicare amount? Because the ATO adds the surcharge to the levy and prints the total on one line, called Medicare levy and surcharge. To see how much of it is the surcharge, look at your M2 answer on the return or rebuild it: your tier rate, applied to taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, for each day you lacked an appropriate level of hospital cover. Who pays no Medicare levy at all? In 2025-26, a single taxpayer whose taxable income is $28,011 or less pays none, and between $28,011 and $35,013 it is reduced. For those entitled to the seniors and pensioners tax offset the lines are $44,268 and $55,335. Exemptions also exist for some medical conditions, foreign residents and people not entitled to Medicare benefits.
